sections.summary: The architecture is coherent, unusually well-specified for plan stage, and its central aesthetic — every guarantee enforced in Postgres, not in app discipline — is the right one and mostly realized. The findings cluster precisely where a guarantee is still comment-true or discipline-true instead of constraint-true: the audit hash chain forks under ordinary concurrency (the one true blocker), the RPC exposure model is self-contradictory in a way that makes the audit ledger forgeable by any authenticated user, non-human actors (workers, cron, agents) have no specified identity and cannot emit audits as written, and every mutable state machine is value-constrained but not transition-constrained. Closing that residue — a chain lock, an api/app schema split with function-privilege revokes, an identity broker for system actors, a transition-guard convention, one composite FK — would make the whole compliance spine provable by pgTAP, which is the product's own thesis applied to itself. Nothing here relitigates a settled decision; the accepted expansions are clean except E3, which needs one environment decision before its reset script collides with the append-only doctrine.

findings.title: audit.compute_chain forks under concurrent same-tenant inserts — the tamper-evidence centerpiece false-alarms under normal load
findings.detail: The trigger (Doc 07 §4) reads the chain head with a plain `select hash … order by id desc limit 1` under default READ COMMITTED isolation. Two concurrent transactions inserting audit events for the same tenant cannot see each other's uncommitted rows, so both read the same head and both write the same prev_hash: the chain forks. There is no serialization anywhere — no advisory lock, no chain-head row lock, no isolation requirement. Concurrent same-tenant audit inserts are not rare: every clock-in emits an audit event in its own transaction, and the Monday 8am shift-start storm is a load scenario the plan itself models (Doc 12 §2 k6). The daily chain-verify job (Doc 09 §7) will then fail recomputation, and audit-chain verify failure is a paging alert (Doc 13 §7) — so the flagship 'provable integrity' control pages a false tamper alarm on the first busy morning, teaching operators to ignore the one alarm that must never be ignored. Compounding: bigint identity values are allocated at insert, not commit, so id order can differ from commit order even without a fork. Doc 12 §3's chain test ('insert sequence → recompute') is sequential-only and cannot catch this.
findings.refs: Doc 07 §4 (audit.compute_chain, trg_audit_chain, audit.audit_event); Doc 09 §7; Doc 13 §7; Doc 12 §2–3; Doc 06 §6.2
findings.recommendation: Amend Doc 07 §4 DDL: serialize chain appends per tenant — either `perform pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext('audit:'||new.tenant_id::text))` at the top of compute_chain, or a `audit.chain_head(tenant_id pk, last_id, last_hash)` table updated under row lock (which also fixes id-vs-commit ordering). Add a required concurrent-insert fork probe to the Doc 12 §3 suite (two parallel transactions, assert linear chain). Specify the verify job's algorithm (per-tenant recompute in id order). Record that all audit writes serialize per tenant — acceptable at ACT scale, and a stated revisit item at SaaS scale.

findings.title: RPC exposure model is self-contradictory, and by Postgres defaults app.emit_audit is a forgeable-ledger endpoint
findings.detail: Doc 07 §1 declares schema `app` = 'functions/helpers (not exposed)'; Doc 08 §1 Lane B is `rpc('app.…')` from supabase-js. PostgREST can only call functions in exposed schemas, so one of these is wrong. If `app` is exposed to make Lane B work, every function in it becomes a callable endpoint — and Postgres grants EXECUTE on new functions to PUBLIC by default; the Doc 07 §2 least-privilege block revokes table privileges only, and says nothing about function privileges anywhere in the conventions. The concrete consequence: `app.emit_audit(p_action, p_entity_type, p_entity_id, p_payload)` is SECURITY DEFINER and inserts directly into audit.audit_event — any authenticated staff account could append arbitrary fabricated events ('form.finalize' on nonexistent entities, fake payloads) into the same hash-chained ledger the product sells as survey evidence. The chain proves append order, not semantic authenticity; a polluted ledger defeats the evidence claim without any 'tampering'.
findings.refs: Doc 07 §1 (schemas convention), §2 (revokes: tables only), §4 (app.emit_audit); Doc 08 §1 Lane B; Doc 06 §10 (integrity thesis)
findings.recommendation: Plan change at S0 (ST-003): split schemas — a dedicated exposed `api` schema containing only the Lane-B RPC catalog, each with explicit per-role EXECUTE grants; `app` stays internal with `revoke execute on all functions in schema app from public, anon, authenticated` plus matching `alter default privileges`. emit_audit becomes uncallable outside definer contexts. Extend the Doc 07 §11 pgTAP matrix with function-privilege probes (every function × role × expected execute). Doc deltas: 07 §1/§2 conventions, 08 §1 Lane B transport string.

findings.title: The non-human identity plane is required everywhere and specified nowhere — as written, workers and agents cannot emit audit events at all
findings.detail: `app.emit_audit` derives tenant via `app.current_tenant_id()` = app_user lookup on `auth.uid()`. Under a service_role context (Edge Function queue consumers — exactly where invariant 6 says service_role lives), auth.uid() is NULL → tenant_id NULL → NOT NULL violation → the worker's transaction aborts. Yet every consequential action must audit (CLAUDE.md invariant 7; Doc 08 §3 marks app.submit_evv and app.satisfy_obligation as 'system'). Doc 09 §2 promises 'system app_user rows per worker (audit attribution)' and Doc 11 §7 requires agents to act 'via a per-agent system user … RLS applies to agents exactly as to humans' — both of which require executing SQL as that user, i.e., a minted JWT with sub = the system user's id. No component in Doc 06 §2's topology mints, scopes, or rotates these JWTs; with Supabase-managed ES256 keys this is not a trivial afterthought (custom signing keys or admin-session generation must be chosen deliberately). This is the nil path of every system-actor data flow: cadence transitions, EVV submission advances, retention sweeps, agent steps.
findings.refs: Doc 07 §3.1 (app.current_tenant_id), §4 (app.emit_audit, audit_event.tenant_id NOT NULL, actor_kind 'system'/'agent'); Doc 08 §3 (system RPCs); Doc 09 §2 (service identities); Doc 11 §7; CLAUDE.md invariants 6–7
findings.recommendation: Add an explicit 'system identity broker' design to Doc 06/09 before S3 (first workers): per-worker and per-agent system app_user rows + a JWT minting path (Supabase custom signing key or admin API session issuance) so workers run user-scoped clients under RLS-as-that-actor; alternatively add a `app.emit_audit_system(tenant, actor, …)` variant executable only by service_role, with the tradeoff (no RLS-as-agent) recorded. pgTAP: a system-actor audit emission test. Draw the broker into the Doc 06 §2 diagram.

findings.title: State machines are value-constrained, not transition-constrained — nothing specified prevents final→draft, complete→pending, reconciled→pending
findings.detail: form_instance.status, shift.status, visit.status, and evv_submission.status are all guarded only by CHECK constraints on the value domain (Doc 07 §5–6). No convention in Doc 07 §1, no trigger, and no column-privilege rule constrains the transition graph — and RLS structurally cannot (policies gate rows, not value changes). The finalize RPC itself has no status precondition: it would 'finalize' a void instance, or re-finalize an already-final one onto a different version; Doc 08 §3's claimed effect 'supersedes prior' appears nowhere in the §5 DDL, and nothing addresses finalizing a non-latest version while newer drafts exist (reachable under the keep-both doctrine). The docs' default-revoke posture blunts the worst case (no UPDATE grant on form_instance is shown), but the enforcement stack the plan is famous for — privilege + trigger + pattern (Doc 06 §6.1) — simply has no transition layer, and ST-022's 'post-final locked' AC has no specified mechanism behind it beyond RPC discipline.
findings.refs: Doc 07 §5 (form_instance, app.finalize_form), §6 (shift, visit, evv_submission CHECKs); Doc 08 §3 (finalize 'supersedes prior'); Doc 06 §6.1; Doc 15 ST-022
findings.recommendation: Add a binding convention to Doc 07 §1: status columns are writable only via RPC (column-level privilege revoke where any UPDATE grant exists) + a generic `app.assert_transition()` BEFORE UPDATE trigger driven by a seeded allowed-edges table, applied to form_instance/shift/visit/evv_submission/ai_interaction/agent_task. Fix finalize_form: require status IN ('draft','in_review'), implement supersede semantics, define latest-version handling. Add a transition-matrix pgTAP family (illegal edge × role → CAREOS_INVALID_TRANSITION) to Doc 12 §3.

findings.title: signature.content_hash equality with form_version.content_hash is comment-enforced; one composite FK makes the e-sign claim constraint-true
findings.detail: Doc 07 §5 defines `signature.content_hash bytea not null -- must equal version.content_hash`. That equality is the entire legal theory of D-004 ('signature binds the exact record version; stronger than a vendor round-trip'), yet it is enforced only by a comment and by trusting app.sign_version to be the sole insert path — and the DDL shown includes no grants or policies for the signature table at all, leaving the insert surface unstated. If any Lane-A insert path exists (or is later granted), a signature row can bind a stale or wrong hash silently.
findings.refs: Doc 07 §5 (public.signature DDL); Doc 08 §3 (app.sign_version), §5 (native e-sign spec); D-004 (Doc 00 §3)
findings.recommendation: Amend Doc 07 §5: add `unique (id, content_hash)` on form_version and a composite FK `foreign key (form_version_id, content_hash) references form_version (id, content_hash)` on signature — the equality becomes unfalsifiable in the database. State signature's grants explicitly (select only; insert via app.sign_version definer context only, per the S1-2 api-schema split). Add a pgTAP probe: insert with mismatched hash must fail.

findings.title: pg_cron cadence tick: silent-stall is unmonitored-by-page, and missed/doubled-tick semantics are unspecified
findings.detail: The entire compliance value proposition executes from one `cron.schedule('careos_cadence_tick', '5 * * * *')` line (Doc 07 §7). Its failure mode is the absence of events — obligations never transition, notifications never fire — which no user reports. Doc 13 §6 lists 'cadence-engine tick health' as a dashboard, but the §7 paging list (availability, DLQ, WAL, audit-chain, canary, auth) omits cadence staleness: a stalled tick is a ticket-at-best. The spec also never states `app.evaluate_compliance()`'s semantics under a missed tick (must be absolute-state catch-up, not window-based) or a doubled/overlapping tick (transition-driven enqueue must not double-fire notifications), and no runbook item verifies cron jobs are live after a PITR restore into a fresh project — a restore that silently drops the scheduler stalls compliance indefinitely.
findings.refs: Doc 07 §7 (cron.schedule, app.evaluate_compliance); Doc 13 §5 (scheduler inventory), §6 (dashboards), §7 (paging list), §8 (restore drills)
findings.recommendation: Three plan edits: (1) evaluate_compliance writes a heartbeat row (last_success_at) and 'tick age > 2× interval' joins the Doc 13 §7 page list; (2) Doc 07 §7 states the contract — idempotent absolute-state evaluation, advisory-lock or single-runner guard, notifications enqueued only on status transition; (3) the Doc 13 §8 restore-drill checklist gains 'verify cron.job entries active and first tick observed'. All by S3 (cadence sprint under the resequence).

findings.title: PowerSync replication slot: the WAL-retention policy decision is missing — a sync-plane outage can take down the production database
findings.detail: Doc 13 monitors 'replication-slot lag, WAL retention headroom' and pages on low headroom, which is good — but monitoring is not a policy. If PowerSync Cloud stalls for an extended period, the slot retains WAL on the primary until disk pressure degrades or downs the system of record: the sync plane (a convenience layer) inverting the 'field ops tolerate total backend outage' story (Doc 06 §9) by taking down the backend itself. The plan never decides the cap-vs-availability tradeoff (bounded slot WAL → forced slot invalidation + fleet re-sync, vs unbounded → disk risk), never confirms the setting is controllable on Supabase, and never plans the slot-loss path at all: PITR restores and platform failovers do not preserve logical slots, so the Doc 13 §8 RTO ≤ 4h silently excludes the time to recreate the slot and fully re-sync every field device.
findings.refs: Doc 13 §6–§9 (monitoring, paging, restore drills, PowerSync runbook); Doc 08 §6.8; Doc 06 §9 (continuity claim); D-003
findings.recommendation: Decide and record (decision-log entry, before S5 mobile): bounded slot WAL retention (verify the knob on Supabase; page well before the cap), with slot invalidation → PowerSync re-snapshot as the accepted failure path. Extend the PowerSync runbook with slot-recreate + fleet full-resync steps; add 'recreate slot, measure Meadowbrook-scale fleet resync time' to the quarterly restore drill so the real RTO includes it.

findings.title: EVV integrity gaps: clock timestamps are client-supplied and unvalidated, and evv_submission has no uniqueness under at-least-once delivery
findings.detail: app.clock_in sets `visit.clock_in_at = p_at` — a device-supplied timestamp — with no server-side sanity check against `received_at`, no shift-window check, and no shift-status check (a caregiver can clock into a cancelled or completed shift, or submit a p_at that says on-time while arriving late). These timestamps feed the federal Cures-Act elements submitted to ISAS and gate billing ('EVV-verified only', Doc 08 §6.4) — this is the system's fraud surface and the spec is silent on it, in contrast to its careful geofence handling. Separately, evv_submission ('per-visit state machine', Doc 06 §6.3) has no unique(visit_id, target): pgmq is at-least-once and both clock RPCs enqueue q_evv_isas, so duplicate submission rows — and duplicate state machines racing against ISAS — are reachable by construction.
findings.refs: Doc 07 §6 (app.clock_in, visit, visit_event.at vs received_at, evv_submission DDL); Doc 08 §6.1; Doc 06 §5 (at-least-once workers), §6.3
findings.recommendation: Amend Doc 07 §6 before S6 (EVV sprint): clock RPCs validate shift status ∈ ('scheduled','in_progress') and flag |p_at − now()| beyond a stated tolerance (larger when p_offline) as an exception, mirroring the geofence never-block-always-flag doctrine; nightly reconciliation includes at-vs-received_at drift. Add `unique (visit_id, target)` to evv_submission and make the submission worker upsert-by-visit. pgTAP: duplicate-enqueue and stale-timestamp probes.

findings.title: The mobile AAL2 / offline-replay auth contract is undefined and currently contradicts invariant 3
findings.detail: CLAUDE.md invariant 3 and Doc 09 §2 require AAL2 for anything PHI, with a 15-minute AAL2 idle re-challenge — yet app.clock_in (writing to PHI-classed visit) checks no AAL2, while form_version_insert's policy does require app.is_aal2(). Now run the flagship offline path: a caregiver documents through a 6-hour basement visit; the queued writes replay headlessly on reconnect under a JWT whose access token (≤1h) must refresh first and whose AAL2 idle window (15 min) has long lapsed. Whether that replay succeeds, silently fails, or strands EVV evidence depends on enforcement mechanics (claim-only check vs session-side idle enforcement) the docs never define. Doc 10 §6's 'failures surface retry, never silent drop' covers the device UI, not the authorization semantics that decide whether retry can ever succeed.
findings.refs: CLAUDE.md invariant 3; Doc 09 §2 (AAL2 idle 15 min, 30d mobile refresh); Doc 07 §5 (form_version_insert requires is_aal2) vs §6 (clock_in does not); Doc 10 §6; Doc 08 §6.8
findings.recommendation: Write the mobile auth contract as a decision-log entry before S5: which writes require AAL2 at replay time, how biometric app-unlock maps to AAL2 step-up/refresh, how the ≤1h token + refresh rotation interacts with multi-hour offline queues, and whether EVV RPCs carry an explicit, documented AAL2 exemption (with rationale) instead of a silent one. Add an airplane-mode E2E case: 6h offline visit → reconnect → replay succeeds or surfaces an actionable re-auth prompt.

findings.title: Realtime channel authorization is unspecified — payload minimization is designed, subscription control is not
findings.detail: Docs 06/08 carefully specify that Realtime channels carry IDs only (`tenant:{id}:visits`, `tenant:{id}:alerts`, `user:{id}:inbox`) with refetch under RLS — but never say who may subscribe. Supabase Realtime channels are not RLS-gated by default; without explicit private-channel authorization, any authenticated principal (including a family-portal user, the lowest-trust tier) could subscribe to the tenant-wide firehose and observe operational metadata: event types, entity types, timing, volume — activity patterns about clients they have no rights to, and a reconnaissance aid for the RLS-probing attacker Doc 09 §7 already worries about. The §11 policy catalog covers domain tables, not the Realtime plane. (Secondary, NOTE-level: N-clients × M-events refetch on the visit board should coalesce client-side; trivial at ACT scale, worth a line in Doc 10 §5.)
findings.refs: Doc 06 §2/§6.4; Doc 08 §1 (Realtime contract); Doc 09 §7; Doc 07 §11 (catalog scope)
findings.recommendation: Extend Doc 08 §1: Realtime uses private channels with authorization policies (RLS on realtime.messages) — family users get no tenant-wide channels; caregivers get user:{id}:inbox plus per-assigned-entity topics; office roles get tenant channels by permission. Add subscription allow/deny cases to the pgTAP-equivalent matrix and an E2E probe (family session attempts tenant channel → denied). Land with the first Realtime feature (live visit board, S4 under the resequence).

findings.title: E3 (Meadowbrook demo tenant) needs an environment decision — a 'reset script' collides with the append-only doctrine if the tenant ever lives in production
findings.detail: Accepted expansion E3 packages Meadowbrook as a permanent demo tenant with a reset script (CEO plan, E3), and the vision names it 'the standing sales stage'. Through Phase 1 demos run on preview/staging (Doc 15 §7) — fine. But if the standing demo tenant is ever placed in production (the natural sales instinct: real URL, real product), the reset script becomes a tenant-scoped hard-delete tool inside the PHI environment — directly against Doc 07 §9's 'no ad-hoc delete path' and mechanically incompatible with [AO] tables (no DELETE grants, forbid_mutation triggers), meaning it could only work by superuser trigger-bypass: a standing footgun one tenant_id typo away from PHI. The CEO plan never states which environment E3 targets; this is the only accepted expansion with a real coupling concern (E1 reads existing spine data, E4 is CI-only, E5 is a storage-only table write, E6 is a UAT artifact — all clean).
findings.refs: CEO plan E3 + Vision (2026-07-21-careos-phase1-resequence.md); Doc 15 §7; Doc 07 §9 ('no ad-hoc delete path'), §1 convention 5 [AO]; D-006
findings.recommendation: One line in the E3 story at S0: the demo tenant lives in staging (or a dedicated non-PHI demo project) for all of Phase 1; reset = environment re-seed, never row deletion. A production demo tenant, if ever wanted for SaaS sales, requires its own decision-log entry with a designed, guarded reset mechanism.

findings.title: audit.audit_anchor primary key is `day` alone — breaks on tenant #2
findings.detail: The anchor table (Doc 07 §4) is `day date primary key` with a tenant_id column, but chains — and therefore daily root hashes — are per-tenant. The moment a second tenant exists (the schema's own stated SaaS path, Doc 06 §6.5), the second tenant's daily anchor violates the PK. Trivial now, annoying to migrate later since anchors are exported to WORM storage.
findings.refs: Doc 07 §4 (audit.audit_anchor); Doc 06 §6.5
findings.recommendation: Change PK to (tenant_id, day) in the S0 migration (ST-003) while the table is empty.

sections.summary: The happy paths of the compliance spine are unusually well specified, but the error/rescue layer is thin and in two places defective in the binding DDL itself: audit.compute_chain forks the hash chain under ordinary concurrency (turning the flagship tamper-evidence control into a false-alarm generator), and app.clock_in checks shift ownership before idempotency, so an offline caregiver whose shift was reassigned gets an unrescuable 'not your shift' for work already done — a lost-EVV/poison-sync path with no defined terminal state. Systemically, the CAREOS_* catalog is five codes plus an ellipsis while every RPC raises bare-text exceptions, leaving ~17 error classes with no code, no rescue action, and no user-facing outcome — which also makes Doc 12 §3's "fail with exact codes" pgTAP assertions unwritable as specced. All fixes are doc/DDL deltas at plan stage; nothing threatens the architecture or the settled decisions.

findings.title: audit.compute_chain forks the hash chain under concurrent inserts — the daily verify job will page false tamper alarms
findings.detail: audit.compute_chain (Doc 07 §4) reads the previous hash with a plain `select hash ... where tenant_id = new.tenant_id order by id desc limit 1` inside a BEFORE INSERT trigger, with no serialization. Two transactions committing concurrently for the same tenant (every RPC calls app.emit_audit in-transaction; Doc 12 §2's own load scenario is the 'Mon 8 am shift-start storm') each read the same committed prev hash, so row N+2.prev_hash != row N+1.hash — a legitimate chain break. The daily chain-verify job (Doc 09 §7) then fails, which is a 24×7 page classified as possible tampering (Doc 13 §7), and the surveyor-facing 'provable integrity' claim (Doc 06 §10) becomes unverifiable in the presence of normal load. Second charter question: a trigger failure aborts the whole business transaction (audit and domain write share one transaction per CLAUDE.md invariant 7) — clock-in fails if the audit insert fails. That IS the right call (no un-audited consequential action; field care survives via the offline queue, Doc 10 §6), but no document says so, and the web/Lane-B rescue for an audit-abort is unspecified. Also, no index supports the prev-hash seek (idx_audit_entity is (tenant_id, entity_type, entity_id, id), not (tenant_id, id)), so every audited write pays a scan.
findings.refs: Doc 07 §4 audit.compute_chain / trg_audit_chain / app.emit_audit; Doc 09 §7 chain-verify job; Doc 13 §7 alert matrix ('audit-chain verify failure' = page); Doc 12 §2 load scenario, §3 audit-chain suite; Doc 06 §6.2, §10; CLAUDE.md invariant 7
findings.recommendation: Amend the Doc 07 §4 DDL: take `pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext(new.tenant_id::text))` at the top of compute_chain (per-tenant serialization is free at ACT's single-tenant scale) and add index `(tenant_id, id desc)`. Add a pgTAP concurrency test (two sessions, same tenant, assert chain linkage) to the Doc 12 §3 audit suite. Add one sentence to Doc 07 §4: 'audit-insert failure aborts the enclosing business transaction by design; field continuity is provided by the offline queue, not by skipping audit.'

findings.title: Offline clock_in replay after shift reassignment: ownership check precedes idempotency check; rejected EVV events have no rescue path and can stall the entire device sync queue
findings.detail: In app.clock_in (Doc 07 §6) the statement order is: (1) `perform ... where s.caregiver_id=auth.uid(); if not found then raise 'not your shift'`, then (2) visit upsert, then (3) the client_event_id idempotency check. Two consequences. (a) Strict idempotency violation: if a clock-in succeeded but the HTTP response was lost and the shift is later reassigned/cancelled, the device's retry errors on an operation that already succeeded — the caregiver sees a failure for a recorded visit. (b) The charter's named gap: a genuinely offline-captured clock-in replayed after reassignment is permanently rejected — a real, federally-required EVV event (six Cures-Act elements, Doc 08 §6.1) is refused with a bare 'not your shift' (no CAREOS_* code, no plain-language copy per Doc 10 §3). This contradicts the plan's own doctrine for the analogous case: out-of-geofence 'never blocks care: it records, flags exception, routes to coordinator review' (Doc 07 §6 note). Downstream, PowerSync's upload queue is ordered — a permanently-rejected write blocks all subsequent uploads; Doc 10 §6 promises 'failures surface retry, never silent drop' but defines no terminal state, park protocol, or coordinator dead-letter for permanently-rejected offline writes, so the honest outcome is an amber banner ('3 updates will send automatically') that never clears, on top of lost care documentation.
findings.refs: Doc 07 §6 app.clock_in (ownership check lines vs idempotency check), visit_event.client_event_id; Doc 08 §6.8 PowerSync writes; Doc 10 §6 offline doctrine; Doc 08 §6.1 Cures elements; Doc 08 §2 catalog (no code for this class)
findings.recommendation: Amend the Doc 07 §6 RPC: move the client_event_id idempotency check to the first statement (return the existing visit for any replay). For a first-time event whose shift no longer belongs to the caller, do not raise: append the visit_event with kind='exception' and payload noting the ownership mismatch, flag for coordinator review (mirror the geofence doctrine), and return a typed result. Add CAREOS_NOT_YOUR_SHIFT to the Doc 08 §2 catalog for the interactive (online) case with caregiver copy. In Doc 10 §6, define the poison-write protocol: after N rejects an item is parked (not dropped), surfaced in the caregiver inbox and a coordinator queue, and the sync queue proceeds past it. Add an airplane-mode E2E case 'clock-in offline → shift reassigned → reconnect' to Doc 12 §4.

findings.title: The CAREOS_* error catalog is five codes and an ellipsis, and the binding DDL doesn't implement it — Doc 12's 'exact codes' pgTAP assertions are unwritable as specced
findings.detail: Doc 08 §2 declares 'code from a stable catalog (CAREOS_APPEND_ONLY, CAREOS_AAL2_REQUIRED, CAREOS_NOT_ON_CARE_TEAM, CAREOS_CREDENTIAL_BLOCK, CAREOS_CONFLICT_KEEP_BOTH, …)' and 'Postgres exceptions map 1:1 to codes' — but the only DDL that emits a code is app.forbid_mutation. finalize_form raises 'not found', 'MFA (AAL2) required', 'not authorized', 'missing required signature(s)'; clock_in raises 'not your shift'; none carry a code, and no convention exists for HOW a raised exception carries its catalog code (message prefix? custom errcode? DETAIL field?). The registry table (artifact) shows ~17 error classes with no code, including: offer-taken, version-append unique_violation, EVV reject reasons, AI budget/capability-disabled, webhook duplicate, revocation partial-failure. Doc 12 §3 requires RPC guard tests to 'fail with exact codes' and Doc 10 §3 requires error copy mapped per error — both are blocked on a catalog that doesn't exist beyond five entries.
findings.refs: Doc 08 §2 error conventions; Doc 07 §4 app.forbid_mutation (only coded raise), §5 app.finalize_form, §6 app.clock_in; Doc 12 §3 RPC guards; Doc 10 §3 voice & tone; CLAUDE.md session ritual ('error codes CAREOS_* (docs/08 §2)')
findings.recommendation: Add a normative appendix to Doc 08 §2: the complete v1 code catalog (start from the artifact's Table A — every 'NO CODE' row gets one), plus the binding raise convention (e.g., `raise exception using errcode='P0001', message='CAREOS_<CODE>', detail=<safe context>` — no PHI in message/detail). Retrofit the two example RPCs in Doc 07 to demonstrate it. Add a CI lint (fits the E4 spec-drift gate) that any `raise exception` in db/ without a CAREOS_ message fails the build.

findings.title: app.clock_out is absent from the binding DDL; no ordering constraint on visit times; EVV enqueue fires at clock-IN before the end-time element exists
findings.detail: Doc 07 §6 shows only clock_in; Doc 08 §3 lists clock_in/clock_out on one catalog row. Clock-out's distinct failure modes are all unspecified: clock-out with no prior clock-in (visit row absent), double clock-out, replay semantics, reassignment mid-visit, and device clock skew — `p_at` is device-supplied and unvalidated, and the visit table has no `CHECK (clock_out_at > clock_in_at)`, so a skewed device can record a negative-duration visit that flows into billable_visit ('EVV-verified only', Doc 08 §6.4). Separately, clock_in enqueues `pgmq.send('q_evv_isas', …)` immediately, but the six Cures-Act elements include begin AND end time (Doc 08 §6.1) — what app.submit_evv does with a visit lacking clock_out is unspecified (spin retries into the DLQ? premature reject?). Also unspecified: the worker-side payer filter — the RPC enqueues every visit including private-pay, while §6.1 says non-Medicaid runs 'minus state submission'.
findings.refs: Doc 07 §6 (clock_in DDL, visit table — missing CHECK; pgmq.send at clock-in); Doc 08 §3 RPC catalog, §6.1 Cures elements + non-Medicaid note, §6.4 billable gate
findings.recommendation: Write app.clock_out into Doc 07 §6 mirroring clock_in (idempotency-first per S2-2, geofence-out, task-checklist confirmation hook). Add `CHECK (clock_out_at is null or clock_out_at > clock_in_at)` plus a sanity window on p_at (e.g., reject/flag >24h future skew as exception, never silently). Specify app.submit_evv preconditions: visits without clock_out are deferred (re-queued with backoff, not retried to DLQ), and the worker filters on payer_type before ISAS submission.

findings.title: EVV state machine: reject→corrected→resubmission loop unspecified; unbounded 'attempt'; a dead-lettered q_evv_isas message contradicts the '100% <24 h queue-drain guarantee' SLO
findings.detail: The evv_submission enum is pending→submitted→accepted|rejected→corrected→reconciled (Doc 07 §6, Doc 08 §6.1), but: (a) there is no transition from 'corrected' back to submission — new evv_submission row or same-row re-advance is unspecified, and the table has neither unique(visit_id) nor a dedup key against external_ref, so duplicate state rows per visit are possible; (b) the charter's named gap — an ISAS reject arriving for a visit that was meanwhile corrected in CareOS (via app.review_visit_exception or new visit_events) has no linkage rule, and a retroactive ISAS adjustment after 'accepted' has no path at all; (c) 'bounded retries' has no bound — `attempt int` exists with no max anywhere; (d) ISAS reject reasons have no taxonomy and no CAREOS_EVV_* codes; (e) Doc 13 §5 sends max-retry messages to the DLQ, but Doc 13 §7's SLO promises '100% <24 h (queue-drain guarantee)' — a DLQ'd EVV message is exactly a visit that will NOT reach ISAS in 24h, and the 'Queue DLQ triage' runbook (Doc 13 §9) is a title with no re-drive SLA.
findings.refs: Doc 07 §6 evv_submission (no unique(visit_id), unbounded attempt); Doc 08 §3 app.submit_evv, §6.1 flow + failure doctrine; Doc 13 §5 DLQ policy, §7 EVV freshness SLO, §9 runbook list
findings.recommendation: Spec the full transition table in Doc 08 §6.1: correction produces a NEW evv_submission row referencing the superseded one (append-only symmetry); old row gets a terminal 'superseded' state; post-accept adjustments enter the same path; add partial-unique index (visit_id) where status not in terminal states. Set max attempts (e.g., 6 with exponential backoff), define the reject-reason taxonomy → CAREOS_EVV_* codes feeding the coordinator exception queue. Give q_evv_isas's DLQ an explicit re-drive SLA (<24h, on-call action) so the SLO and the DLQ policy stop contradicting each other.

findings.title: Direct Lane-A inserts on form_version bypass correct_form's mandatory reason (including on FINAL instances); version_no races have no rescue; finalize vs concurrent append is unadjudicable because correct_form has no contract
findings.detail: Doc 07 §5 grants `insert on form_version to authenticated` with a policy checking only tenant + AAL2 + author_id — not instance status, not version sequence. So after finalize, any care-team member can append a form_version with kind='edit' and note NULL directly via Lane A, bypassing correct_form's 'reason mandatory' guard (Doc 08 §3) — the column comment itself admits 'required by RPC' only. The autosave design (Doc 10 §4, drafts every 3s) makes heavy direct-insert use likely, and two concurrent autosaves (web + offline sync replay) computing next version_no collide on unique(instance_id, version_no) → raw 23505 with no code and no specified retry, silently contradicting the 'Saved ✓ 2:41 PM' promise. Meanwhile finalize_form locks only the form_instance row; a version append doesn't take that lock, so finalize can land on a non-latest version with a dangling unsigned draft after 'final' — and whether that's legal is undecidable because correct_form's contract (allowed source states, effect on instance status, whether re-finalize/re-sign is required, can you correct a draft) appears nowhere in Docs 07/08.
findings.refs: Doc 07 §5 form_version grants + form_version_insert policy + note column comment + unique(instance_id, version_no); app.finalize_form (instance-only lock); Doc 08 §3 correct_form row; Doc 10 §4 autosave/finalize UX
findings.recommendation: Route all version appends through one RPC (app.append_form_version) that assigns version_no under the instance lock, enforces status rules (final ⇒ kind='correction' + reason NOT NULL), and revoke the direct insert grant — or keep Lane A for drafts but add a BEFORE INSERT trigger enforcing the same rules. Define correct_form's state contract in Doc 08 §3 (source states, resulting instance status, re-sign requirement per §5's 'any content change = new version = new signature'). Add codes CAREOS_VERSION_CONFLICT (retry-with-recompute client behavior) and CAREOS_CORRECTION_REASON_REQUIRED; extend the ST-021/ST-022 pgTAP set accordingly.

findings.title: app.revoke_user_access spans four systems and has no partial-failure or re-run semantics — the flagship ≤15-min control is a happy-path spec
findings.detail: Doc 09 §2 defines revocation as: ban auth user + revoke refresh tokens (Supabase Auth admin API) + set status/separated_at + end assignments (Postgres) + expire PowerSync sync buckets (PowerSync API) + invalidate push tokens (Expo). These cannot share a transaction. Nothing specifies behavior when step 3 of 5 fails: does the DB commit stand while the device keeps syncing (ambiguous access during exactly the window the 15-min control is measured on), or does anything roll back? No idempotent re-run, no per-step verification, no alert-on-incomplete, no error code. The drill (ST-014, Doc 12 §4) verifies the happy path only.
findings.refs: Doc 09 §2 session revocation row; Doc 15 ST-014; Doc 12 §4 access-revocation E2E; Doc 08 §3 (RPC listed only implicitly)
findings.recommendation: Respec as a verified saga in Doc 09 §2: DB transition commits first (perimeter denial is instant via RLS — status!='active' already fails app.has_perm), then external steps run as queued, idempotent, individually-audited jobs with a completion checklist; incomplete-after-N-minutes pages on-call. Make app.revoke_user_access safely re-runnable and give the drill a forced-partial-failure case (e.g., PowerSync API down).

findings.title: SMS 'ACCEPT' → app.accept_offer has no authenticated principal (conflicts invariant 6), and the first-accept race loser has no code, no reply, no UX
findings.detail: Doc 08 §7's sequence shows a Twilio inbound 'ACCEPT' reply resulting in app.accept_offer, whose guard is 'offeree' (Doc 08 §3). But the inbound path is webhook → q_integrations → worker: the worker holds no offeree JWT, and CLAUDE.md invariant 6 / Doc 06 §4 forbid service_role in request paths — the identity bridge is unspecified. Separately, 'first-accept wins (row lock); rest expire' defines the winner but not the loser's experience: no CAREOS_OFFER_TAKEN code, no in-app copy, and an SMS responder who lost the race gets no defined reply at all (Twilio content rules in §6.2 constrain what it may say, but something must be said).
findings.refs: Doc 08 §3 accept_offer row, §7 sequence diagram, §6.2 Twilio content rule; Doc 06 §4 lane rules; CLAUDE.md invariant 6
findings.recommendation: Spec the identity bridge in Doc 08 §7: cleanest is that the SMS carries a per-offer single-use signed deep link into the app, and accept happens in-app under the caregiver's own JWT (SMS reply 'ACCEPT' merely triggers a nudge); if true reply-to-accept is required, define a scoped system-actor path with explicit on-behalf-of attribution in the audit event and a documented exception to invariant 6. Add CAREOS_OFFER_TAKEN + loser copy for both surfaces ('This shift was just filled — thanks for responding').

findings.title: 'No worker ever serves a client with a lapsed license — by construction' only holds at assignment time; nothing re-checks between assignment and the visit
findings.detail: assert_schedulable gates app.assign_shift (Doc 07 §8, Doc 08 §3). But a credential that expires — or is verification-rejected via app.verify_credential — AFTER assignment triggers only a cadence-engine obligation/notification (Doc 07 §7): no specified sweep flags or unassigns the affected future shifts, and app.clock_in performs no credential check, so the caregiver clocks in normally. The guarantee as worded (Doc 07 §8, echoing Doc 01 G5) is enforcement language for what is actually a notify-and-hope path. Also unspecified in the same family: assign_shift on a shift in a terminal/in-progress status, and two coordinators assigning concurrently (the 409/keep-both convention is defined for Lane-A row_version writes, not for this RPC).
findings.refs: Doc 07 §8 assert_schedulable + the 'by construction' claim, §7 cadence engine, §6 app.clock_in (no credential check); Doc 08 §3 assign_shift/verify_credential rows; Doc 08 §2 concurrency convention
findings.recommendation: Add to Doc 07 §8: on credential expiry/rejection, the cadence transition enqueues a shift-sweep job that flags affected future shifts (status→open or 'blocked' + coordinator notification, never silent unassign of an in-progress visit). clock_in gains a soft check — lapsed credential records the visit and flags kind='exception' (care never blocks, consistent with S2-2's doctrine). Specify assign_shift's status preconditions and its concurrent-assignment behavior (row lock, second writer gets CAREOS_SHIFT_TAKEN or the keep-both flow — pick one explicitly).

findings.title: Deepgram mid-stream failure: partial-transcript recovery unspecified for the live path
findings.detail: Doc 08 §6.5 and Doc 10 §6 define the OFFLINE fallback (record locally → batch on reconnect) but not the mid-stream failure: a live streaming session that drops halfway leaves a partial transcript, and nothing states that audio is also retained locally DURING live streaming — if it isn't, the dictation tail is unrecoverable, violating 'progress is never lost' (Doc 10 §1). No defined merge of partial transcript + recovered audio, no error code, no user copy.
findings.refs: Doc 08 §6.5 Deepgram; Doc 10 §1 principle 3, §6 voice notes; Doc 11 §10 ('voice → type' covers provider-down, not mid-stream)
findings.recommendation: One-line doctrine in Doc 10 §6: the device always records locally while streaming; on stream failure, the full local audio is batch-submitted and its transcript replaces the partial (partial shown meanwhile, labeled). Copy per Doc 10 voice: what happened, what's saved, what happens next.

findings.title: Webhook idempotency keys on the pgmq message id, not the provider event id; Checkr/Twilio have no missed-webhook backstop
findings.detail: Doc 06 §5 makes workers idempotent on the queue event id — but a provider redelivering the same webhook (allowed inside Doc 08 §2's 5-min timestamp window, and normal provider behavior on slow 2xx) enqueues a SECOND pgmq message with a new id, so the dedup key doesn't cover the actual duplicate. Consequence: e.g., double-processed Checkr report.completed. Conversely, a webhook lost during a provider or endpoint outage has a reconciliation backstop for QBO (drift report) and ISAS (nightly recon) but none for Checkr or Twilio delivery status — an onboarding candidate can stall silently.
findings.refs: Doc 06 §5 worker idempotency; Doc 08 §2 inbound webhook rules, §6.2 Twilio, §6.3 Checkr; Doc 13 §5
findings.recommendation: Amend Doc 08 §2: handlers dedupe on the provider's native event id (persisted 48h alongside Lane-C idempotency keys) before enqueue. Add a nightly Checkr status-poll reconciliation for in-flight candidates (mirrors the ISAS pattern); Twilio delivery-state gaps surface via the existing notification-delivery table as an aging alert.

findings.title: AI failure matrix lacks partial-progress and stale-approval rows; the AI error class has no CAREOS_* codes
findings.detail: Doc 11 §10 covers provider-down, low-confidence, schema-invalid (one repair retry → human), budget, and guardrail-trip well. Missing: (a) multi-page packet extraction failing at page 17/30 — resume-from-page vs restart-job is unspecified even though the review UI 'presents progressively' (Doc 11 §4), so the reviewer-visible state after mid-job failure is undefined; (b) T1 stale approval — a plan drafted, then approved after the world changed (offered caregiver now unavailable, shift cancelled): 'T1 executes post-approval' (Doc 11 §3) with no execution-time revalidation gate; (c) no catalog codes for the class (budget-exceeded, capability-disabled, extraction-failed), tying into S2-3.
findings.refs: Doc 11 §3 (T1 executes post-approval), §4 step 7 + latency targets, §10 matrix; Doc 08 §2 catalog
findings.recommendation: Add two rows to the Doc 11 §10 matrix: 'partial pipeline failure → job checkpoints per page, resume from last good page, reviewer sees explicit `17/30 processed — resuming` state' and 'stale T1 approval → execution re-validates preconditions; on mismatch, halt and re-propose (never execute against changed state)'. Extend the S2-3 catalog with CAREOS_AI_BUDGET_EXCEEDED, CAREOS_AI_CAPABILITY_DISABLED, CAREOS_AI_EXTRACTION_FAILED.

sections.summary: The security architecture is genuinely strong at the perimeter it names — RLS-as-perimeter, append-only + hash chain, explicit grants, allowlist PHI-minimization, and a clean parameterized RPC surface with no dynamic SQL. But two claims do not survive contact with the published DDL/ops assignments: the ≤15-minute revocation control is actually delivered by JWT expiry (≤1h) because `app.on_care_team` and the `created_by` policy branch never check user status, and the service_role custody matrix is incoherent with docs/13's assignment of q_ai_jobs consumption to Vercel Cron (no sanctioned credential exists for those workers). Around the edges, four asserted controls are phrases without designs — AV scanning, family-portal scoping, export controls on the thin S4 survey packet, and the E5 knowledge-capture loop's poisoning/PHI hygiene — each needing a plan change before its consuming sprint.

findings.title: Revocation is delivered by token expiry (≤1h), not the claimed ≤15 min: `app.on_care_team` and the `created_by` policy branch never check user status
findings.detail: Threat: separated (possibly hostile) staff retain PHI read access after `app.revoke_user_access` runs. Likelihood M (separations are routine; for-cause separations are the exact threat case), Impact H (PHI exposure + a false compliance-evidence claim). Docs/09 §2 claims target ≤15 min and 'beats the proposed 2026 rule's 1-hour bar', and ST-014's drill AC says 'separated test user fully dead ≤15 min'. The mechanism list (ban auth user, revoke refresh tokens, set status='separated', end assignments, expire PowerSync buckets) kills new logins, token refresh, mobile sync, and every `app.has_perm` path (which checks `u.status='active'`). It does NOT kill: (a) `app.on_care_team` (docs/07 §3.1) — no join to `app_user.status`, and `care_team_assignment.ends_on` is a `date`, so setting ends_on=today still satisfies `ends_on >= current_date` until midnight; (b) the `fi.created_by = auth.uid()` branch of `form_version_select` (docs/07 §5) — no status check at all. ES256 JWTs are verified statelessly by PostgREST via JWKS (docs/09 §2); a banned user's already-issued access token stays valid up to 1h, and no per-request denylist/introspection is specified anywhere. Net: a separated caregiver can curl PostgREST directly with their live JWT and read their assigned clients and every form they authored for up to ~60 minutes — the drill as scripted (which tests fresh sessions) would pass while the control fails.
findings.refs: Doc 09 §2 (Session revocation, JWTs rows); Doc 07 §3.1 `app.on_care_team`, `app.has_perm`; Doc 07 §5 `form_version_select` created_by branch; Doc 07 §3 `care_team_assignment.ends_on date`; Doc 15 ST-014 AC; Doc 09 §9 NPRM readiness '≤1-h revocation ✔ (15-min target)'
findings.recommendation: Three DDL/plan changes: (1) add an `app_user.status='active'` predicate to `app.on_care_team` and to the `created_by` branch (or a shared `app.is_active_user()` wrapper used by every policy); (2) make assignment end-of-access instant-capable (timestamptz `ended_at`, or revoke sets ends_on to yesterday with the true separation moment kept in `separated_at`); (3) either shorten staff access-token TTL to ≤10 min or add a revocation-epoch check reachable from RLS. Then rewrite the ST-014 drill AC to assert web/PostgREST access is dead using a STILL-LIVE pre-revocation access token, not a fresh session. Until then, stop stating ≤15 min in auditor-facing text.

findings.title: Worker-identity incoherence: Vercel Cron is assigned to consume `q_ai_jobs` but no sanctioned credential exists for it — the custody matrix and the ops plan cannot both hold
findings.detail: Threat: the S7 builder (an AI agent under CLAUDE.md) hits an impossible constraint and resolves it by putting `service_role` or direct DB creds in Vercel env — exactly what docs/09 §5 forbids ('Never in: Vercel runtime env') — or invents an ad-hoc auth path. Likelihood H (the contradiction is guaranteed to be encountered at S7), Impact H (a service_role key in Vercel runtime is a total-RLS-bypass credential in the request-serving platform). The chain: docs/13 §5 and docs/06 §5.2 assign AI orchestration — 'Vercel Cron: AI job orchestrator (q_ai_jobs)', 'extraction, drafting, agent steps' — to Vercel. Consuming pgmq and reading intake documents requires DB-privileged access; there is no user JWT in a cron invocation. Docs/09 §5 allows DB creds only in Edge Function secrets and CI; docs/08 Lane C says 'Never holds service_role'. Docs/09 §2 gestures at 'Service identities: system app_user rows per worker; machine creds scoped + rotated (§5)' — but §5 has no row defining what those machine creds are or where a Vercel worker's credential lives. Same gap applies to `app.submit_evv` whose guard is just 'system' with no defined mechanism for presenting as system under RLS.
findings.refs: Doc 13 §5 (Vercel Cron: AI job orchestrator q_ai_jobs); Doc 06 §5.2; Doc 08 §1 Lane C hard rule; Doc 09 §5 custody matrix (service_role, DB direct credentials rows); Doc 09 §2 Service identities row; Doc 08 §3 `app.submit_evv` guard 'system'; CLAUDE.md invariant 6
findings.recommendation: Ratify a machine-identity pattern as a decision-log entry (D-010) before S6/S7 planning. Two coherent options: (a) move ALL queue consumption to Supabase Edge Functions (which may hold service_role per the matrix), with Vercel handling only stateless orchestration invoked BY Edge Functions carrying scoped context; or (b) define a dedicated low-privilege Postgres role per worker class (grants limited to its queues + accessor RPCs, no RLS bypass) with its credential added as an explicit custody-matrix row. Add the `system`-actor authentication mechanism (how `app.submit_evv` verifies its caller) to docs/07 §3.1, and a pgTAP probe that the worker role cannot read PHI tables directly.

findings.title: '/api/v1/intake/documents': 'AV scan on ingest' is a phrase, not a design — no scanner, no quarantine ordering, no zip-bomb/polyglot/type-allowlist defenses
findings.detail: Threat: file-borne malware delivered to the coordinator/reviewer browser via the side-by-side review UI, pipeline DoS via decompression bombs or 1000-page files, and polyglot files (valid PDF + valid script) reaching the LLM and reviewer. Likelihood M (fax/email sources make this an unauthenticated external content channel into the tenant), Impact M-H (workstation compromise of the highest-privilege office users; extraction-pipeline outage). Status: GAP. Docs/09 §4 asserts 'AV scan on ingest' in one table cell; docs/11 §4's ingest pipeline (upload → `document` row → bucket → `q_ai_jobs`) never mentions scanning, so as sequenced the extraction model and the reviewer can consume the file before/without any scan. Supabase Storage has no native AV — this is a build item with no story in docs/15, no engine choice, no quarantine state, and no vendor-register row (a third-party scanner ingesting PHI files would itself need a BAA per docs/09 §6). Docs/08 §4 specifies no MIME allowlist, size cap, or page cap for the multipart POST (the '≤30 pp' figure in docs/11 §4 is a latency target, not a limit). The STRIDE table's only related row is 'Prompt injection via faxes', which covers the LLM-instruction vector, not the file-handling vector.
findings.refs: Doc 09 §4 Files row; Doc 11 §4 steps 1-2 (no AV stage); Doc 08 §4 `/api/v1/intake/documents`; Doc 07 §9 `document.source` includes 'fax','email'; Doc 09 §10 (no malicious-upload row); Doc 15 (no story)
findings.recommendation: Add an ingest-hardening story to S7 (or S2 if any upload path ships earlier): quarantine bucket → scan (ClamAV in an Edge Function keeps it in-boundary; any external scanner requires a vendor-register + BAA entry) → promote → only then enqueue `q_ai_jobs`; hard MIME allowlist (pdf/jpeg/png/tiff), reject archives outright, max bytes and max pages enforced at the Route Handler; reviewer UI renders server-rasterized page images, never the original file inline. Add 'malicious file upload' as a docs/09 §10 row.

findings.title: Family-portal authorization is unspecified while its RPCs and tables ship in Phase-1 schema — and family MFA posture contradicts the AAL2-for-PHI invariant
findings.detail: Threat: IDOR between family members — of different clients, or of the same client with different consent scopes (`family_member_link` carries a scope; `app.grant_family_access` takes 'client, user, scope') — yielding wrongful PHI disclosure, a reportable breach. Likelihood M at ship time, Impact H. Status: GAP. There is no scoping helper for `kind='family'` users anywhere in docs/07: `app.on_care_team` covers staff assignments only, and no `family_member_link` policy or `app.is_family_of()` predicate is specified, yet the grant/revoke RPCs sit in the v1 Lane-B catalog and docs/10 §2 lists `/family` with core screens in the v1 inventory while docs/15 puts the portal at Phase 2+ (a scope contradiction in itself). Separately: docs/09 §2 says family 'MFA strongly encouraged, required for any document access' — but the visit calendar and updates feed are PHI, and CLAUDE.md invariant 3 / docs/07 policies require `app.is_aal2()` for PHI. As written, either family users see nothing (policies require aal2 they don't have) or an unwritten AAL1-family exception exists. The STRIDE table has no family-portal row.
findings.refs: Doc 08 §3 `app.grant_family_access`/`revoke_family_access`; Doc 07 §10 family portal row (`family_member_link`, `portal_consent`); Doc 07 §3.1 (no family helper); Doc 09 §2 MFA row; CLAUDE.md invariant 3; Doc 10 §2 `/family` v1 inventory vs Doc 15 §2 Phase-2+ epic; Doc 09 §10 (no family row)
findings.recommendation: Decision-log entry now resolving (a) whether any `/family` surface is Phase 1 (align docs/10 §2 with docs/15) and (b) the family AAL posture — recommended: MFA mandatory for all family PHI access, satisfying invariant 3 without exceptions. Before any family surface ships: add `app.is_family_of(client, required_scope)` (status-checked, consent-gated via `portal_consent`) to docs/07 §3.1, a policy suite scoped by link + consent scope, pgTAP matrix rows including two-families-same-client and revoked-consent cases, and a family-IDOR row in docs/09 §10.

findings.title: E5 founder-knowledge capture creates a Brain corpus-poisoning and PHI-hygiene path that the injection hardening does not cover
findings.detail: Threat 1 — poisoning: docs/11 §5's hardening (retrieved-content-as-data, zero mutating tools, cite-or-abstain) defeats instruction-injection but not authority poisoning: a malicious or compromised account that can write `knowledge_document` rows gets its content served later as the agency's cited, authoritative answer ('what's our med-error procedure?'). E5 (CEO plan, S1) specifies no write permission, no review gate before corpus inclusion, and the docs/11 §7 red-team suite tests malicious-fax injection, not corpus poisoning. Threat 2 — PHI: six sprints of free-text founder answers (S1→S7) accumulate before the PHI-minimizer and canary suite exist (S7); founders answer client-specific questions ('when is Ms. Z due?') in exactly the style docs/11 §5 says must NOT be pre-embedded, yet the S7 ingest step ('curated founder answers') defines no curation mechanics, classification pass, or `scope`/`sensitivity` tagging discipline for captured content. Likelihood M, Impact M-H (wrong authoritative answers in a clinical-adjacent Q&A surface; PHI embedded into `knowledge_chunk` with broader read scope than the source entity). Status: GAP — partially mitigated by cite-or-abstain (citations at least make the poisoned source visible).
findings.refs: CEO plan E5 / Accepted Scope S1 bullet; Doc 11 §5 (ingestion, injection hardening, 'operational-data grounding is not pre-embedded'); Doc 11 §7 red-team suite (fax vector only); Doc 07 §10 knowledge row (`scope`, `sensitivity`); Doc 09 §10 (no poisoning row)
findings.recommendation: Amend E5's story ACs: (1) `knowledge_document` writes require a named permission (`knowledge.capture`), and rows carry `status` in ('captured','curated','retired') — only 'curated' rows (founder/RN-approved) are eligible for S7 embedding; (2) capture-loop rule stated in UI copy and enforced at S7 ingest: answers are policy-level, never client-specific — S7 ingest runs a PHI-classification pass and quarantines hits for rewrite; (3) extend the docs/11 §7 red-team suite with corpus-poisoning cases (planted instruction-bearing and factually-adversarial curated docs); (4) add a poisoning row to docs/09 §10.

findings.title: The thin S4 survey packet (E1) is the product's largest single PHI aggregation and its ACs do not bind the docs/09 §10 export controls (watermark, volume alerts, bundle custody)
findings.detail: Threat: exfiltration via a legitimate feature — one permission (`compliance.export`) yields a client's (or, per the RPC signature's 'client?/agency' arg, the whole agency's) multi-year evidence bundle behind a forwardable bearer signed URL. Likelihood M (insider or compromised office account), Impact H. Status: partially mitigated — the RPC row carries the permission gate and audit (docs/08 §3), and signed URLs are ≤5-min TTL. GAP for the rest: docs/09 §10's exports row promises 'volume anomaly alerts + watermarked, audited packets', and docs/09 §7 wires 'mass-export patterns' detection 'at launch' — but E1 moves the feature to S4 while those detections have no sprint anchor, and a deliberately 'thin' implementation will naturally omit watermarking, the anomaly rule in the log store, and custody of the generated bundle (which bucket, what classification/retention, whether each download is attributable). Nothing in the CEO plan's E1 bullet or dependency validation mentions inheriting these controls.
findings.refs: CEO plan E1 / Accepted Scope S4 bullet; Doc 08 §3 `app.export_survey_packet` ('client?/agency, range'); Doc 09 §10 exports row; Doc 09 §7 detections 'wired at launch'; Doc 09 §4 signed-URL row; Doc 07 §9 `document.source='generated'`
findings.recommendation: Write E1's ACs to enumerate the inherited controls explicitly: `compliance.export` gate (present); audit payload includes requester, scope, date range, and a manifest hash of bundle contents; every packet page watermarked (requester + timestamp + 'confidential'); generated bundle stored as `document(source='generated', classification='phi')` with retention; signed URL ≤5 min and re-mint audited per download; the mass-export anomaly rule ships in the same sprint as the feature (S4), not 'at launch'. Consider restricting the agency-wide variant to a second approver until Phase 2. Anything consciously deferred gets a decision-log note, not silence.

findings.title: The builder/platform console identity plane (Supabase, Vercel, GitHub, Anthropic org accounts) is outside the threat model — and for a one-human team it is the real perimeter
findings.detail: Threat: compromise of Salim's Supabase org, Vercel team, GitHub, or Anthropic console account = full control of the PHI database, deploy pipeline, secrets, and AI configuration — bypassing every in-product control (RLS, AAL2, audit chain all run below platform-admin altitude; only the WORM audit anchors survive as a detection backstop). Likelihood L-M, Impact H (total). Status: GAP. Docs/09 §2 governs application identities only; §5 governs secret values; §3 access reviews cover app roles; docs/13 §4's supply-chain items (pinned actions, lockfiles, secret scanning) cover code, not the humans-on-consoles. The tabletop scenario is 'founder's account compromised' (the client), not the builder. The design doc confirms team = Salim + AI agents, which concentrates this risk in exactly one identity and adds a second uncovered vector: agent-authored code reaching main under single-human review (Open Question 4 covers promotion approval but not console/account hardening).
findings.refs: Doc 09 §2/§3/§5/§8 tabletop scenarios/§10 supply-chain row; Doc 13 §4; design doc Constraints (team reality) + Open Question 4; Doc 13 §8 (WORM anchors as the only surviving backstop)
findings.recommendation: Add a 'platform/builder identities' subsection to docs/09 §2: FIDO2/hardware-key MFA mandatory on Supabase, Vercel, GitHub, and Anthropic consoles (no TOTP-only, no SMS); org member lists folded into the quarterly access review; GitHub: branch protection on main, environment-scoped secrets, required review even for agent-authored PRs per the Open-Question-4 resolution; add 'builder console compromise' to docs/09 §10 and as a third tabletop scenario; include the CI/CD chain in the S8 pentest scope.

findings.title: Lane-B contract drift in the binding DDL: `app.clock_in` performs no AAL2 or tenant validation despite docs/08's 'Every RPC validates AAL2 + permission' rule
findings.detail: Threat: an AAL1 session (staff mid-enrollment, pre-MFA — explicitly 'AAL1-limited (no PHI)' per docs/09 §2) can execute a consequential, security-definer state change: `app.clock_in` checks only `s.caregiver_id=auth.uid()`, then writes `visit`/`visit_event`, reads the client's geocoded home location, and returns the full visit row — with no `app.is_aal2()` check, no tenant re-check, and no shift-status check (a cancelled shift can be clocked into). Likelihood L (requires a caregiver account paused mid-enrollment or an aal-downgraded session), Impact M. The larger risk is pattern propagation: docs/07 is the template corpus the coding agents copy from, and the pgTAP plan (docs/12 §3) tests clock_in for idempotency and geofence but not AAL2 — so the drift is invisible to the test gate too. `finalize_form` does it right; `clock_in` silently doesn't, and no exemption is documented.
findings.refs: Doc 08 §1 Lane B hard rule; Doc 07 §6 `app.clock_in` body; Doc 09 §2 AAL1-limited enrollment; Doc 12 §3 RPC-guard list (AAL2 asserted for finalize_form only)
findings.recommendation: Either add `app.is_aal2()` + tenant + shift-status guards to `app.clock_in`, or document an explicit field-usability exemption (offline EVV replay rationale) as a decision-log entry — silence is the only wrong option. Add a pgTAP convention test: every `app.*` RPC either asserts AAL2 or appears on a reviewed exemption manifest; the manifest is a generated artifact like `db/policies.md` so drift fails the build.

findings.title: Realtime channel authorization is unspecified — tenant-scoped channel names alone don't prevent cross-tenant subscription
findings.detail: Threat: an authenticated user of tenant A subscribing to `tenant:{B}:visits` / `tenant:{B}:alerts`. Payloads are IDs-only by doctrine, so the leak is metadata (entity IDs, event tempo — e.g., visit cadence, alert volume), not PHI. Likelihood L, Impact L-M today (single real tenant in Phase 1), but the plan's own multi-tenant SaaS path and the E3 permanent Meadowbrook demo tenant make tenant isolation a standing property; docs/08 §1 defines the channels but no authorization mechanism (Supabase Realtime requires explicit private-channel authorization — e.g., RLS on `realtime.messages` — otherwise broadcast channels are joinable by any authenticated client). Status: GAP, low stakes now, cheap to close by construction.
findings.refs: Doc 08 §1 Realtime paragraph; Doc 06 §3 Realtime row and §6.5 multi-tenancy; CEO plan E3
findings.recommendation: One sentence added to docs/08 §1: channels are private, authorized via Realtime RLS with the same `app.current_tenant_id()` predicate as domain tables; add a pgTAP/E2E probe that a tenant-A JWT cannot join a tenant-B channel. Land it in S0 with the schema core so it's never retrofitted.
