## Artifact 2 — The audit-chain fork under concurrency (why S6-1 is CRITICAL)

```
  Chain head at t0:  ... ──► E3 (hash H3)          single tenant (ACT), normal load

  T1: app.clock_in                     T2: app.finalize_form        (concurrent txns)
  ─────────────────                    ────────────────────
  emit_audit -> trigger:               emit_audit -> trigger:
    SELECT hash ORDER BY id DESC        SELECT hash ORDER BY id DESC
      -> sees H3                          -> sees H3        (T1 uncommitted = invisible)
    INSERT E4  prev_hash = H3           INSERT E5  prev_hash = H3
    COMMIT                              COMMIT

  Resulting "chain":        E3 ◄─── E4          <-- FORK: two children of H3
                             ▲
                             └───── E5

  Daily verify job (Doc09 §7): walk by id: E5.prev_hash (H3) != E4.hash  -> FAIL
      -> pages "audit-chain verify failure" (Doc13 §7)  == false tamper alarm
  OR: verification written fork-tolerant -> real tampering becomes undetectable.
  Either branch defeats the control. No attacker required — Monday 8am is enough.

  Fix: serialize append per tenant (pg_advisory_xact_lock on tenant_id) +
       DB-concurrency test: N parallel emit_audit -> assert exactly one child per hash.
```

sections.summary: At ACT's scale (~100 staff, ~10^3 visits/month) the platform has enormous raw headroom, and the plan does define budgets and a k6 storm test — the posture is fundamentally sound. But the review found one correctness-grade defect in the binding DDL (the audit hash chain races under any concurrent same-tenant writes, forking the chain the compliance story depends on) and a cluster of specced defaults that fight the plan's own budgets: RLS helper calls that execute per-row with no initplan idiom and partial indexes that cannot serve them, autosave specced to mint a full-content form_version every 3 seconds, AI jobs picked up by minute-granularity cron against a 60-second extraction p95, and web mutations routed through cold-startable Vercel functions against an 800 ms write p95. All are cheap to fix at plan stage; several would otherwise surface only at the S8 load test, after six sprints of code sits on top of them.

findings.title: audit.compute_chain races under concurrent writes — the hash chain forks; the fix creates a per-tenant serialization ceiling that must be specced and measured
findings.detail: The BEFORE INSERT trigger (Doc 07 §4) reads `SELECT hash FROM audit.audit_event WHERE tenant_id = new.tenant_id ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1` with no locking of any kind. Under READ COMMITTED, two concurrent audited transactions in the same tenant both see the same committed tail row, both set the same prev_hash, and the chain forks: row N+2's prev_hash no longer equals hash(row N+1). Doc 12 §3's chain verification ('insert sequence → recompute hashes → assert linkage') recomputes by id order, so verification fails — and 'audit-chain verify failure' is a 24×7 paging alert in Doc 13 §7. Concurrency ≥2 is guaranteed in normal operation: Monday-8am clock-ins (Doc 12 §2's own load scenario), and especially the PowerSync post-outage queue drain, where dozens of devices replay queued clock_in RPCs in parallel, each calling app.emit_audit in-transaction (CLAUDE.md invariant 7). Doc 12 §3's specced chain tests are sequential-insert only, so pgTAP as planned will not catch this; the k6 storm at S8 will — six sprints late, as a page. The standard fix (pg_advisory_xact_lock keyed on tenant_id inside the trigger) is correct but serializes ALL audited writes per tenant for the remainder of each transaction: ceiling ≈ 1000 ms ÷ (ms from audit insert to COMMIT). A clock_in transaction tail of 5–15 ms gives ~65–200 audited writes/s/tenant — comfortably above ACT's 3× peak (bursts ≤ ~10/s), but it is now a real architectural ceiling that the multi-tenant SaaS path (Doc 06 §6.5) inherits, and long-running Lane-B transactions that emit audit early would hold the lock for their full duration.
findings.refs: Doc 07 §4 (audit.compute_chain, trg_audit_chain, app.emit_audit); Doc 12 §3 (audit-chain suite — sequential only) and §2 (k6 Mon-8am storm); Doc 13 §7 (audit-chain verify failure = page); CLAUDE.md invariant 7; Doc 08 §6.8 (PowerSync parallel write drain)
findings.recommendation: Amend the Doc 07 §4 DDL now: add `perform pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext(new.tenant_id::text))` (or a per-tenant sequence row locked FOR UPDATE) as the first statement of compute_chain, and emit audit as late as possible in RPC transactions to minimize lock-hold. Add a (tenant_id, id DESC) index for the tail lookup (the existing idx_audit_entity cannot serve ORDER BY id within a tenant once tenant count > 1). Add two specced tests: a pgTAP/concurrency test (two sessions, same tenant, assert unbroken chain) and a k6 assertion that chain verification stays green under the 3× storm. Record the measured ceiling in Doc 06 §9 as a named budget.

findings.title: RLS helper cost is unmanaged: no initplan-caching idiom specced anywhere, and both care_team_assignment partial indexes cannot serve app.on_care_team's predicate
findings.detail: Two concrete defects in the binding DDL. (1) Policies call app.has_perm(...), app.current_tenant_id(), and app.is_aal2() bare (e.g. client_select_scoped, form_version_select, Doc 07 §5). These are STABLE SECURITY DEFINER SQL functions — not inlinable — so Postgres executes them per candidate row; has_perm alone is a 3-table EXISTS (~30–80 µs/call). The standard Supabase/Postgres mitigation — wrapping constant-argument calls in `(select app.has_perm('x'))` so the planner hoists them to a one-shot InitPlan — appears nowhere: not in Doc 07 §1 conventions, §3.1, §11, nor in Doc 12's test plan. (2) app.on_care_team filters `client_id = p AND user_id = auth.uid() AND (ends_on IS NULL OR ends_on >= current_date)`, but both specced indexes (idx_cta_user_active, idx_cta_client_active) are partial on `WHERE ends_on IS NULL`. A partial index is usable only when the query predicate implies the index predicate; `ends_on >= current_date` rows are outside it, so the planner cannot use either index and every on_care_team call seq-scans care_team_assignment. Net cost model: a roster/chart query pays candidate_rows × Σ(helper costs); at ~500 clients this is tens of ms (budget-consuming), and on the fastest-growing table — form_version, whose policy adds an EXISTS over form_instance plus on_care_team per row, over rows amplified by S7-3 — chart-history reads degrade past the 400 ms read p95 at roughly 10^3–10^4 candidate rows. This is the single largest determinant of whether Doc 06 §9's read budget holds, and it is currently unspecced.
findings.refs: Doc 07 §3.1 (app.has_perm, app.on_care_team, security definer helpers); Doc 07 §3 (idx_cta_user_active / idx_cta_client_active — `where ends_on is null`); Doc 07 §5 (client_select_scoped, form_version_select); Doc 07 §1/§11 (conventions & policy catalog — no initplan idiom); Doc 06 §9 (reads p95 < 400 ms)
findings.recommendation: Add a binding convention to Doc 07 §1: every constant-argument helper in a policy MUST be wrapped `(select ...)` (initplan form); regenerate the 63-policy catalog accordingly. Fix the index: replace the two partial indexes with a composite btree on (user_id, client_id, ends_on) — or keep the partials but change the helper/data model so ended assignments always set ends_on (making `IS NULL` the sole active predicate). Add a CI plan-shape guard (EXPLAIN-based pgTAP assertion: no seq scan on care_team_assignment from on_care_team; helpers appear as InitPlan) so the idiom cannot regress, mirroring the policy-drift gate in Doc 07 §11.

findings.title: Autosave is specced to mint a full-content form_version row every 3 seconds — an append-only table amplified by 2–3 orders of magnitude, degrading history reads, RLS scans, storage, and sync
findings.detail: Doc 10 §4 binds autosave as 'debounced 3 s + on-blur → draft form_versions (kind edit)', and Doc 07 §5 makes form_version an [AO] table storing the complete answers jsonb (`content`) plus content_hash per row. A 45-minute RN assessment with continuous editing yields on the order of 10^2–10^3 versions, each a full snapshot (5–50 KB for a real assessment) — per session. At ~1k visits/month plus assessments, form_version plausibly reaches 10^5–10^6 rows/year with gigabytes of near-duplicate jsonb. Consequences compound: the history timeline UI (ST-021/ST-024) reads all versions per instance; the form_version_select policy pays per-row EXISTS + on_care_team (S7-2) over the amplified row count; PITR/backup volume grows; and if 'charts-lite' (S7-4) syncs any version history, mobile initial sync balloons. None of the budgets in Doc 06 §9 or the k6 plan in Doc 12 §2 model this write rate. Note this does NOT require relitigating append-only: versions stay immutable; the defect is the version-cut policy (every 3 s of typing) conflated with keystroke-recovery.
findings.refs: Doc 10 §4 (autosave → draft form_versions); Doc 07 §5 (form_version [AO], content jsonb, unique(instance_id, version_no)); Doc 15 ST-020/ST-021/ST-024; Doc 06 §9; Doc 12 §2
findings.recommendation: Plan decision (Doc 10 §4 + Doc 07 §5 delta, one decision-log entry): separate 'recovery autosave' from 'version'. Options, either compliant with the append-only invariant: (a) cut form_version rows only at meaningful checkpoints (on-blur of a section, navigation, explicit save, max every N minutes), with in-between keystroke state held in local/client draft storage — 'navigating away never loses input' is preserved by the client draft; or (b) a single mutable form_draft working row per (instance, author) — drafts are pre-version working state, not records of consequence — coalescing autosaves, versioned on checkpoint. Add a form_version row-growth assumption to the k6 model and a Meadowbrook fixture with a realistically-amplified instance so history-timeline p95 is tested against real row counts.

findings.title: PowerSync initial-sync payload is unbounded: 'charts-lite' is never defined and no initial-sync budget exists (only delta < 5 s is budgeted)
findings.detail: Doc 06 §9 budgets sync delta < 5 s post-reconnect; Doc 10 §6 scopes a device to 'their shifts ±14 d, their clients' charts-lite, templates, their credentials/inbox' — but 'charts-lite' has no table/column enumeration, no row windows, and no size budget anywhere in the package. ST-033's AC verifies scope correctness (only assigned clients), not scope size. The unbounded cases are real: Meadowbrook itself ships an edge persona with '90 days of visits' and a 'client with 4 caregivers' (Doc 12 §7); if charts-lite includes visit/visit_event history or any form_version rows (amplified per S7-3), a caregiver with 6 clients pulls an initial sync in the tens of MB on first login — on the plan's own reference device, a mid-tier Android on 4G — while ST-032's 'cold start < 2 s to Today offline' silently presumes that sync already completed. First-login experience for the hardest adoption cohort (design doc: caregivers onboard at S5–S7) is exactly where an unbudgeted multi-minute sync costs adoption.
findings.refs: Doc 10 §6 ('charts-lite', shifts ±14 d); Doc 06 §9 (sync delta < 5 s — only sync budget); Doc 08 §6.8 (sync rules mirror assignments); Doc 15 ST-032/ST-033 ACs; Doc 12 §7 (Meadowbrook 90-day personas); design doc S5 (mobile foundation sprint)
findings.recommendation: Spec a sync-rule manifest as a first-class reviewed artifact (like db/policies.md): exact tables, columns, and row windows per bucket — e.g., forms sync current_version only, visits windowed to ±14 d matching shifts, no version history on device. Add two budgets to Doc 06 §9: initial sync < N MB and < M s on 4G mid-tier Android (propose 10 MB / 60 s), and a CI check that syncs a Meadowbrook worst-case persona (4-caregiver client, 90-day history) against the manifest and asserts the budget. Wire this into ST-033's AC at S5.

findings.title: Web mutations are specced through Vercel Server Actions, where cold starts at ACT's low traffic threaten the 800 ms write p95; lane assignment, Fluid compute, and region pinning are unspecced
findings.detail: Doc 08 §1 puts consequential writes on Lane B (`rpc('app.…')` via supabase-js — browser to PostgREST directly, no Vercel function in the path), but Doc 10 §5 specs 'Server Actions for mutations with optimistic UI + rollback toasts' — which routes web mutations through Vercel serverless functions. These two specs are in tension, and the performance consequences differ sharply: a Next.js App Router function with the app's dependency graph (supabase-js, zod, AI SDK in the bundle) cold-starts in roughly 300 ms–1 s+, and at ACT's request volume (a ~100-person agency with long idle gaps, especially off-hours and early morning) the cold fraction of requests can exceed 5–20% — enough for cold starts alone to consume or bust the 800 ms write p95 at exactly p95. Additionally, no doc pins Vercel function regions to Supabase's US-East (Doc 13 §8 names Supabase's region; nothing constrains Vercel's), and RSC pages doing sequential queries would pay any cross-region penalty per round trip against the 400 ms read p95 and 2.5 s LCP. Vercel's Fluid compute (which largely amortizes cold starts) is never mentioned. The k6 plan (Doc 12 §2) tests budgets but doesn't say which lane each journey exercises, so a green k6 on Lane-B paths could mask a red Server-Action path.
findings.refs: Doc 08 §1 (Lane B = supabase-js rpc, direct); Doc 10 §5 ('Server Actions for mutations'); Doc 06 §9 (writes p95 < 800 ms, LCP < 2.5 s); Doc 13 §6 (synthetic probe — warms one path only) and §8 (US-East primary); Doc 12 §2 (k6 budgets)
findings.recommendation: Resolve the lane ambiguity in Doc 08 §1 with one sentence: field-surface and interactive mutations call Lane B directly from the client; Server Actions are reserved for Lane-C orchestration (integrations/AI). Add to Doc 13: enable Vercel Fluid compute, pin function region to the Supabase region, and note that anything using direct Postgres connections from functions must go through the pooler. Amend Doc 12 §2 so k6 budgets are measured and reported per-lane (A/B direct vs C via Vercel), with cold-start percentiles broken out.

findings.title: q_ai_jobs consumed by Vercel Cron polling makes the 60 s extraction p95 arithmetically infeasible — pickup latency alone is ~0–60 s
findings.detail: Doc 13 §5 assigns the AI job orchestrator (q_ai_jobs) to Vercel Cron, whose minimum schedule granularity is one minute. A job enqueued uniformly within the polling interval waits mean ~30 s, p95 ~57 s, before any work begins — against Doc 11 §4's targets of 'single-doc extraction p95 < 60 s' and a review UI that 'presents progressively (per-page streaming)'. The budget is consumed by queue pickup before the first model token. Doc 06 §5 already contains the better pattern for Edge Function consumers ('invoked on schedule + on-demand') but does not extend it to the Vercel-side AI worker. This lands at S7 in the resequence — the sprint where the founder-visible moment is 'intake packet → extraction review' — so a sluggish pipeline directly degrades a headline demo.
findings.refs: Doc 13 §5 ('Vercel Cron: AI job orchestrator (q_ai_jobs)'); Doc 11 §4 (extraction p95 < 60 s, ≤30 pp < 5 min, progressive review); Doc 06 §5 (on-demand invocation pattern, Edge Functions only); design doc S7 (founder-visible moment)
findings.recommendation: Spec kick-on-enqueue for q_ai_jobs: the enqueuing action (Lane-C route or an Edge Function reacting to the outbox) immediately invokes the orchestrator over HTTP with the job id, with Vercel Cron retained purely as a sweeper for missed/retried jobs. One line in Doc 06 §5 and Doc 13 §5; verify in the S7 E2E journey that extraction p95 is measured enqueue-to-draft, not model-call-only.

findings.title: The geocoding pipeline behind client.geo is unspecified — no provider (a PHI-egress vendor decision), no async job, and a NULL geo silently turns every clock-in into an exception
findings.detail: EVV geofencing depends on client.geo ('geocoded service location', Doc 07 §5), and ST-012 mentions 'geocoding' in one word — but no document specifies which geocoding service converts addresses to coordinates, when it runs (client create? address change?), or what happens on failure. This is simultaneously a vendor-register gap (a client's home address is PHI; sending it to a geocoder adds a data flow that CLAUDE.md forbids without a docs/09 §6 register entry, and Doc 10 §5's map note covers only tiles, not geocoding) and a concrete runtime defect in the binding DDL: if geo IS NULL, app.clock_in computes `st_dwithin(NULL, …)` → NULL → `case when v_in then … else 'exception' end` routes EVERY visit for that client to the exception queue with within_geofence_in = NULL, flooding coordinator review with false exceptions — the exact failure mode Doc 05/FR-AI-032's 'never silently reject' doctrine tries to avoid, inverted into 'always silently flag'. Per-clock-in ST_DWithin itself is fine (single-row comparison, no spatial index needed).
findings.refs: Doc 07 §5 (client.geo, app.clock_in `case when v_in`); Doc 07 §6 (within_geofence_in nullable); Doc 15 ST-012 ('CRUD, geocoding, RLS'); Doc 10 §5 (map/tiles note — geocoding absent); Doc 08 §6 (integration list — no geocoder); CLAUDE.md ('never add a vendor… not in the docs/09 §6 register')
findings.recommendation: Spec the pipeline: choose the provider deliberately (self-hosted Nominatim/Census keeps addresses in-boundary at zero marginal vendor risk; a commercial geocoder requires a DPA/BAA-equivalent register entry), run geocoding as an async outbox job on client create/address change with a visible 'location not verified' state on the client record, and amend app.clock_in to branch on geo IS NULL: record the event with a distinct 'no_geofence_configured' marker (not 'exception'), so ungeocoded clients don't flood the review queue. Add a pgTAP case for the NULL-geo path.

findings.title: Cadence tick: the partial index serves status transitions, but obligation materialization has no uniqueness key — the hourly tick can duplicate obligations and must anti-join outside the index
findings.detail: Verification the charter asked for: the transition query (status IN ('open','at_risk') AND due_at threshold) implies idx_oblig_open's predicate (status IN ('open','at_risk','overdue')), so that half of app.evaluate_compliance() is served — confirmed fine. The materialization half is not: '(re)materialize obligations' (Doc 07 §7 prose) must answer 'does an obligation already exist for (rule × subject × period)?', but compliance_obligation has no unique constraint or period key at all, and satisfied/waived rows fall outside the partial index — so the dedup check scans an ever-growing table (satisfied obligations accumulate for the 6-year retention life), and worse, nothing structurally prevents the hourly tick from inserting duplicate obligations after any logic slip or concurrent tick overlap (pg_cron does not guarantee non-overlap if a tick runs long; the 15-min escalation sweep in Doc 13 §5 touches the same rows). Duplicate obligations mean duplicate notifications and a polluted obligations dashboard — the week-8 founder-visible deliverable in the resequenced plan.
findings.refs: Doc 07 §7 (compliance_obligation DDL — no unique key; idx_oblig_open partial predicate; evaluate_compliance prose; cron.schedule hourly); Doc 13 §5 (15-min escalation sweep, pg_cron); design doc S3 ('week ~8: obligations dashboard'); Doc 12 §3 (cadence tests — dates/transitions, not idempotency)
findings.recommendation: Add a period identity to the DDL: a period_key column (derived deterministically from rule + anchor date) with UNIQUE (tenant_id, rule_id, client_id, employee_id, period_key) — treated as NULLS NOT DISTINCT or via coalesce-expression index — and spec materialization as INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, making the tick idempotent by construction and turning the dedup check into an index probe. Add a pgTAP case: run evaluate_compliance() twice (and two overlapping ticks) → identical obligation set.

findings.title: HNSW + RLS post-filtering can silently shrink Brain recall for permission-restricted users; iterative scan settings and per-role retrieval evals are unspecced
findings.detail: knowledge_chunk retrieval runs 'as the requesting user' under RLS (Doc 11 §5) over an HNSW index (Doc 07 §10). Postgres applies RLS as a filter over the index scan's candidate stream: an HNSW scan returns ~ef_search nearest candidates, and if a restricted user (sensitivity-scoped chunks, or a future second tenant) can see only a small fraction, most candidates are filtered out and the query returns fewer than k results — degraded recall that looks like 'the Brain doesn't know', inflating the abstain rate Doc 11 §5 treats as a coverage signal. At ACT's Phase-1 corpus (mostly agency-wide policy chunks, thousands of rows) practical risk is low, which is why this is a NOTE — but the eval plan (Doc 11 §9: groundedness, citation validity) never tests retrieval recall per-role, so the failure mode would be invisible until a sensitive-scope corpus or tenant #2 exists.
findings.refs: Doc 07 §10 (knowledge_chunk, hnsw + GIN, RLS same-as-source); Doc 11 §5 (retrieval as requesting user; abstain-rate signal) and §9 (eval gates — no per-role recall); Doc 06 §6.5 (multi-tenant path)
findings.recommendation: One paragraph in Doc 11 §5: set pgvector iterative index scanning (hnsw.iterative_scan = relaxed_order) on the retrieval RPC, size ef_search for the worst-case visible fraction, and add a per-role retrieval-recall fixture to the §9 eval set (restricted persona must retrieve its full entitled top-k from a corpus where it can see ~10% of chunks).

findings.title: Keyset pagination is binding only for Lane C — Lane A (supabase-js), which carries most list reads, defaults to offset pagination (.range()), and ranked endpoints can't keyset at all
findings.detail: Doc 08 §2 declares keyset pagination but scopes the conventions as 'binding for Lane C; Lane B mirrors where applicable' — Lane A is unbound, and supabase-js's idiomatic pagination is offset-based (.range(from, to)), which degrades linearly with depth and skews under concurrent inserts (a real concern on append-only, fast-growing tables like form_version and audit views). Separately, two specced surfaces cannot keyset by nature: universal ⌘K search (relevance-ranked, Doc 10 §2) and Brain hybrid RRF retrieval (Doc 11 §5) — both are fine as bounded top-N but should say so, or the 'keyset, max 200' convention reads as violated. Minor at ACT scale; cheap to close now while the api-client package is unbuilt.
findings.refs: Doc 08 §2 (pagination convention + 'binding for Lane C' scoping) and §1 (Lane A); Doc 10 §2 (⌘K search); Doc 11 §5 (RRF retrieval); Doc 07 §5 (form_version growth per S7-3)
findings.recommendation: Extend Doc 08 §2's pagination rule to Lane A explicitly, provide a keyset helper in packages/api-client (cursor on (created_at,id) or (id) per resource) with an ESLint rule banning bare .range() outside it, and annotate ranked endpoints as bounded top-N (no pagination) in the conventions table.

findings.title: Realtime IDs-only broadcasts specify no refetch granularity or coalescing — a Monday-8am board with dozens of visit updates multiplies into N×M RLS-expensive refetches
findings.detail: Doc 08 §1 specs channels broadcasting {entity_type, entity_id, event} with clients refetching via Lane A — correct for PHI safety, but silent on granularity. If the live visit board (Doc 10 §2) refetches its whole query per event, a burst of ~30–90 clock-ins (Doc 12 §2's storm at 3×) times every subscribed office client yields hundreds of board-sized queries in minutes, each paying the per-row RLS helper costs from S7-2 — read amplification the 400 ms p95 wasn't budgeted for. The payload already carries entity_id, so single-entity refetch is the natural implementation; the plan just never says it, and TanStack Query is mentioned (Doc 10 §5) without an invalidation doctrine.
findings.refs: Doc 08 §1 (Realtime contract); Doc 10 §2 (live visit board) and §5 (TanStack Query); Doc 12 §2 (Mon-8am storm); Doc 06 §9 (reads p95)
findings.recommendation: Add two sentences to Doc 08 §1: clients refetch by entity_id (single-row under RLS), never whole-collection, and burst events coalesce client-side (e.g., 1–2 s invalidation window) with a periodic full reconcile. Include the storm-driven board in the k6/E2E scenario so the refetch pattern is exercised at 3× peak.

sections.summary: The observability spine is genuinely strong where the plan looked: three-stream logging with an allowlist scrubber and planted-PHI canary, hash-chained audit with WORM anchors, and the record-integrity question ("did this note change after signing?") is answerable in minutes from the database alone. The systemic hole is that the plan detects loud failures and is structurally blind to silent ones: nearly every liveness signal (cadence tick, anchor export, chain-verify, queue-health probe) runs inside the same pg_cron/database failure domain it is supposed to watch, and the Doc 13 §7 paging matrix omits scheduler liveness entirely — the compliance engine can die for days without a page. Compounding this, the alerting/on-call design was written for a 3-4 engineer rotation that the ratified design doc says does not exist; for a one-human operator, silence must mean "provably fine," which requires deadman-based alerting plus an operator/founder-visible "engines green" surface — none of which is currently planned. Finally, the bug-reconstruction path dead-ends at request correlation (Doc 08 promises audit_event.payload.request_id; the binding DDL never captures it), field devices with stuck sync queues are invisible server-side, and all three accepted expansions (E1/E4/E5) shipped into the plan with zero metric definitions.

findings.title: No deadman switch for the compliance engine or evidence jobs — silent scheduler death is unpaged and self-blind
findings.detail: The paging matrix in Doc 13 §7 is written as an exhaustive list (page = availability burn, DLQ growth, replication/WAL headroom, audit-chain verify failure, canary-PHI hit, auth-anomaly cluster) and it contains no liveness alert for any scheduled job. Doc 13 §5's pg_cron roster — cadence tick (hourly, the COMAR compliance engine per Doc 07 §7 `cron.schedule('careos_cadence_tick',…)`), obligation escalation sweep (15 min), audit-anchor export (daily 02:00), retention sweep, queue-health probe — can all silently stop (pg_cron job errors land in cron.job_run_details unread; jobs can vanish or double after a PITR restore) and nothing in the plan pages. Worse, every watcher shares the watched component's failure domain: the queue-health probe is itself a pg_cron job, and 'audit-chain verify failure' pages only if the verify job runs and fails — a verify job that stops running produces no signal at all (absence-of-signal ≠ success). The anchor-export case is acute: audit.audit_anchor.exported_at simply stays NULL on failure, the in-DB chain-verify still passes, and the tamper-evidence backstop that Doc 13 §8 explicitly places 'outside the primary vendor' silently degrades to nothing. Doc 13 §6 lists 'cadence-engine tick health' as a dashboard — but a dashboard is not an alert, and on a one-human team (design doc premise P5) nobody is watching it at 3am. A cadence engine dead for days before a survey means un-materialized 48-hr/annual/45-90-120-day obligations — the exact founder-memory failure mode CareOS exists to replace, now with false confidence attached. The plan's own external synthetic probes (login+read canary, mobile sync canary) prove the pattern is understood for the request path; it was never applied to the async/compliance path.
findings.refs: Doc 13 §5 (cron roster), §6 (dashboards vs alerts), §7 (page list omits scheduler liveness), §8 (anchors as out-of-vendor backstop); Doc 07 §4 audit.audit_anchor (nullable exported_at), §7 careos_cadence_tick; Doc 09 §7 (daily chain-verify); design doc premise P5
findings.recommendation: Add a job-heartbeat contract to the plan: every pg_cron and Vercel-cron job writes a completion row (job key, ran_at, ok, duration) to an OPS table AND emits a log line; an EXTERNAL deadman monitor (log-store alert asserting 'success line seen within window', or dead-man-snitch-style ping — anything outside the Postgres failure domain) pages on: cadence tick silent >2h, escalation sweep silent >1h, anchor export stale >26h (exported_at-based), chain-verify silent >26h, retention sweep silent >8d. Extend the Doc 13 §7 page list with these rows and add the anchor-export check to Doc 09 §7's detections. Land it in S0 with ST-004 (the observability skeleton) so it guards every subsequent sprint; enumerate the Doc 13 delta in D-009.

findings.title: Queue-consumer silent wedging: a dead consumer grows main queues while the DLQ — the only paged metric — stays empty
findings.detail: Doc 13 §5/§7 page on 'DLQ depth and oldest-message age'. But the failure mode that produces an empty DLQ is the dangerous one: Edge Function consumers are 'invoked on schedule + on-demand' — if the invoker breaks (schedule misconfigured, function deploy broken, invocation auth expired), q_notifications/q_evv_isas/q_integrations/q_ai_jobs grow unboundedly while zero messages ever reach max-retry, so the DLQ never grows and nothing pages. Main-queue 'depths & lag' appear only as dashboards (Doc 13 §6). The 'queue-health probe (5 min)' in §5 has no specified contract: what it asserts, what thresholds, where alerts route — and per S8-1 it runs on pg_cron, inside the same DB as the queues it probes. Meanwhile the EVV SLO ('100% of visits submitted <24h — queue-drain guarantee', §7) and notification SLO (p95 <60s) both silently depend on consumers being alive; the 24h/72h EVV aging alerts are the only backstop, and they cover one queue of four.
findings.refs: Doc 13 §5 (consumer invocation model, unspecified queue-health probe), §6 (queue depths as dashboard only), §7 (page list = DLQ only; EVV/notification SLOs); Doc 06 §5 (named queues + DLQs)
findings.recommendation: Specify the queue-health probe contract in Doc 13: per-queue oldest-message age and depth-growth thresholds (e.g., q_notifications age >5 min, q_evv_isas age >30 min, any queue age >1h) that PAGE, not dashboard; add per-consumer last-successful-run heartbeats feeding the S8-1 deadman so 'consumer never invoked' is detected within one period; assert in the chaos-drill suite (Doc 12 §5) that killing a consumer's invoker produces a page within 15 min.

findings.title: Field-device sync telemetry is blind: '3 updates will send automatically' exists only on the device, and the EVV queue-drain SLO is unmeasurable for stuck devices
findings.detail: Doc 10 §6's offline doctrine is excellent UX (queued-count banner, per-item status, 'failures surface retry, never silent drop') — but every one of those signals lives on the device. Nothing exports PHI-safe client sync telemetry: no queue depth, no oldest-queued-item age, no last-successful-sync timestamp, no upload-failure counts. Doc 13 §6's 'sync health' covers the server side only (PowerSync replication slot lag, WAL headroom) and the hourly 'mobile sync canary' tests the sync service, not any real device; Sentry 'session health' captures crashes, not queue state. Consequence one: a caregiver's device wedged with queued visit_events for five days is server-side indistinguishable from 'caregiver never clocked in' — the visit row does not exist until sync, so the EVV aging alerts (24h/72h, Doc 13 §7) never fire and the '100% <24h queue-drain guarantee' SLO reads green while being violated (unsynced visits are absent from its denominator). Consequence two: field-device debugging is reduced to phoning a caregiver in a basement and asking them to read their screen — against the product's own persona doctrine. The live visit board gives a human backstop for missed clock-ins, but nothing for queued notes, task completions, or partially-synced visits.
findings.refs: Doc 10 §6 (offline states, on-device only); Doc 13 §6 (server-side sync health, mobile sync canary), §7 (EVV freshness SLO); Doc 09 §7 (allowlist: IDs/codes/durations — a beacon fits it); Doc 07 §6 (visit created server-side only via clock_in RPC)
findings.recommendation: Add to the S5 mobile-foundation scope (PowerSync epic, Doc 15 E07): a periodic OPS-class sync heartbeat beacon — device_id, app version, queue_depth, oldest_queued_at, last_sync_at, failure_count; explicitly no PHI, designed against the Doc 09 §7 allowlist and covered by the canary suite — posted whenever connectivity exists; a server-side device-last-seen registry; an alert 'device has queued writes older than N hours' (page for EVV-bearing queues, ticket otherwise); and a device-health chip on the office live visit board so the coordinator sees stuck devices before payroll does. Re-state the EVV queue-drain SLO measurement to include device-side age.

findings.title: Request-ID correlation promised in Doc 08 is unimplemented in the binding DDL — the 3-week-old-bug walk dead-ends at 'which request caused this'
findings.detail: Doc 08 §2 (binding): 'requests carry X-Request-Id … propagated through OTel traces and into audit_event.payload.request_id.' The binding DDL cannot deliver this: app.emit_audit (Doc 07 §4) takes only caller-supplied payload, and the Lane-B RPCs pass domain fields only (finalize_form → version_id; clock_in → within_geofence/offline). No mechanism is specified for a PostgREST-invoked RPC to see the header (the standard path — reading current_setting('request.headers') — appears nowhere), and audit_event's ip/user_agent columns likewise have no population path in any RPC. This matters precisely because the scrubbing allowlist (IDs, codes, durations — Doc 09 §7) makes the request-id nearly the only join key between an audit event and the scrubbed logs/traces that explain it: in the charter's scenario walk (see artifact), steps 1-5 (what happened to the record) are answerable from the DB alone — a real strength — but step 6 (which request/code path produced the anomalous version; was it a duplicate offline replay, a wrong-version render, a sync artifact) has no navigable path from audit row to trace. Sub-gap: retention is stated for log drains (1-yr hot / 6-yr archival) but never for OTel traces or Sentry events — if trace retention lands at a vendor-default 30 days, a '3-week-old bug' is answerable and a 5-week-old one is not, by accident rather than decision.
findings.refs: Doc 08 §2 (headers/request-id promise); Doc 07 §4 app.emit_audit signature + audit_event ip/user_agent columns, §5 finalize_form, §6 clock_in (payloads carry no request context); Doc 09 §7 (allowlist + log retention tiers); Doc 13 §6 (traces 'exported to the BAA'd store' — no retention stated)
findings.recommendation: Amend the Doc 07 DDL: app.emit_audit reads x-request-id (and ip/user-agent) from the PostgREST request.headers GUC with a defined fallback for direct/worker sessions (workers set a local GUC per job); pgTAP asserts every emitted event carries request_id. Define the mobile/PowerSync-upload equivalent (client_event_id already exists — bind it into the audit payload). State trace/Sentry retention explicitly in Doc 13 §6 with a floor ≥90 days. Enumerate the DDL delta in D-009.

findings.title: All three build-visible accepted expansions (E1, E4, E5) entered the plan with zero observability definitions
findings.detail: E1 (survey packet at S4): app.export_survey_packet is an async 'evidence bundle job → signed URL (audited)' (Doc 08 §3) with no latency target, no job-failure alert, and no metrics (volume, duration, actor), despite being simultaneously (a) the wedge's sharpest founder-felt moment per the CEO plan, (b) the numerator of the E6 mock-drill KPI ('N surveyor requests answered in M minutes'), and (c) a named exfiltration vector whose mitigation Doc 09 §10 states as 'volume anomaly alerts' — an alert with no defined metric source anywhere in Doc 13 §6's dashboard list. A packet job that fails silently while a surveyor stands in the office is the single worst possible observability miss for this product. E4 (spec-drift CI gate): gate hit rate is untracked; with an agent workforce, hit rate is the leading indicator of whether agents are drifting from the corpus — the gate's entire justification ('enforcement beats prompting'). E5 (founder-knowledge capture from S1): no metric tracks questions captured / answered / pending-age; the loop can silently stall for six sprints and the first anyone learns is a cold Brain at S7 — defeating E5's stated purpose ('Brain launches warm with six sprints of curated founder answers').

findings.title: audit_anchor primary key is day-only while the chain is per-tenant — anchor machinery breaks at the second tenant, which E3 makes real

But audit.audit_anchor is declared 'day date primary key' with tenant_id as a mere column (Doc 07 §4) — the second tenant's anchor insert for any day collides on the PK and the export job errors or skips. Combined with S8-1 (no anchor-export failure alert), the likely real-world presentation is: anchors quietly stop exporting the day tenant #2 appears, and nobody notices until an auditor asks for the WORM trail.

findings.title: The alerting/on-call design is written for a 3-4 engineer rotation the ratified design doc says does not exist
findings.detail: Doc 13 §7: 'On-call: weekly rotation across the 3–4 engineers, comp-time policy, escalation to lead in 15 min unacked.' The approved design doc (premise P5, confirmed) states the real team is Salim + AI coding agents, and it gave explicit substitutes for the other multi-human controls (two-person promote, CODEOWNERS — Open Question 4) but is silent on on-call and alerting. As written, the escalation path is meaningless (the on-call IS the lead), 24×7 paging assumes someone else covers sleep and the founder-style 'vacation test' the product sells is failed by its own operator model, and an uncurated page list guarantees alert fatigue for one human — the condition under which the S8-1 silent failures become permanent. For a solo operator the design principle inverts: silence must mean 'provably fine' (deadman-based, per S8-1), pages must be few and each auto-remediation-attempted first (restart consumer, re-run tick, retry export — then page), and everything else lands in a daily digest.

Owner Salim, decide by end of S0 alongside the promotion-control decision.

findings.title: Founder- and operator-visible 'all engines green' surface — the cheapest trust feature the plan doesn't have
findings.detail: The exec dashboard (Doc 10 §2: census, staffing, compliance heat, alerts) shows business state but nothing shows that the machines producing it are alive: last cadence tick, queue drain ages, last anchor export, EVV pipeline funnel freshness, AI capability flags, sync health. For a product whose entire thesis is provable trustworthiness — and an operator model of one human — a small system-status strip turns silent failures into founder-visible facts, gives the E6 mock-survey drill its liveness evidence ('the system shows you it has been running'), and is a standing demo asset on the Meadowbrook tenant. Once S8-1's job_heartbeat table exists, this surface is a read-only card over data already collected — near-zero marginal cost, and it is the observability-as-joy answer for one human: every morning, one glance says either 'all engines green' or exactly which runbook to open.

findings.detail: Doc 13 §9's ten runbooks cover the loud failures well (DLQ triage, ISAS outage, WAL recovery, restore, break-glass). Missing, mapped to failure modes this section surfaced: (1) cadence-engine stall & backfill — how to re-run safely after a gap, recompute missed at_risk/overdue transitions, and avoid duplicate notifications; (2) audit-chain verify FAILURE response — the §7 page exists but no runbook: tamper-vs-bug triage, scoping via anchors, evidence preservation, SEV-1 fork (the 'malicious insider edits history' tabletop in Doc 09 §8 proves the scenario is anticipated; the drilled runbook is not); (3) stuck field device / unsynced EVV recovery — recovering queued events without loss, manual_attested fallback, client_event_id reconciliation; (4) scheduler recovery after PITR restore — pg_cron job state is database state; the quarterly restore drill should assert schedules are alive and nothing double-fires; (5) survey-packet export failure during a live survey — a documented manual SQL evidence script for the one moment the product cannot fumble; (6) Meadowbrook demo-tenant reset failure before a sales demo (E3 makes the reset script a standing business dependency). Sections 1-2's findings may add more; the runbook list should be reconciled against the full review's failure-mode inventory at S8 planning.

sections.summary: The deployment spine is genuinely strong for a plan-stage package — trunk-based with per-PR full stacks, expand-migrate-contract, PITR bookmarks, quarterly restore drills, an exit runbook. But it rests on two capability assumptions the chosen platforms do not honor by default: (1) that a Supabase branch + Vercel preview reproduces the async backbone (pg_cron invocation secrets, Vault contents, Storage buckets, and especially Vercel Cron — which fires only on production deployments — do not replicate), while the CI pipeline, release-gated E2E journeys, and the founder demo rhythm all assume previews are "a full working stack"; and (2) that a PITR bookmark is a meaningful rollback for a bad migration, when append-only tables plus daily WORM-exported anchors make PITR a data-destroying, chain-diverging event with no reconciliation runbook. Four smaller deploy-time contracts are unwritten: feature-flag bootstrap semantics, a mobile compatibility-window policy, Server-Action deploy skew, and the interaction between OQ4's no-prod-promotions interim rule and ST-004's prod-hardening ACs.

findings.title: Preview stacks silently lack the async backbone the plan's CI, E2E, and demo strategy depend on
findings.detail: Doc 13 §1 claims 'Every PR = a full working stack URL' (Vercel Preview + Supabase branch), and Doc 13 §4 runs 'e2e (Playwright vs preview)' pre-merge with Doc 12 §2 API/contract tests 'against preview env'. But the async backbone (Doc 06 §5, Doc 13 §5) does not replicate into that stack: (a) Vercel Cron fires only on a project's production deployment — the q_ai_jobs orchestrator, nightly reconciliation, and config-drift check never run on any Vercel preview, and never on staging either if staging is a non-production 'Vercel env' of the same project as Doc 13 §1's wording implies; (b) Supabase preview branches run migrations (so pgmq queues and cron.schedule rows like careos_cadence_tick, Doc 07 §8, exist) but Vault secrets and Edge Function secrets do not copy, so pg_cron→Edge-Function invocation wiring is dead on every branch; (c) Storage buckets/objects ('client-docs', 'hr-docs', 'intake-inbox', Doc 07 §media) do not copy into branches, breaking the intake-from-document E2E upload path; (d) there is no per-branch PowerSync instance, ever. Consequences: the Doc 12 §4 journeys that are async-dependent (open-shift fill with agent→SMS mock, EVV submission state machine, exception review) cannot pass per-PR as pipelined; either CI is red from S3 onward or the async paths get quietly excluded from pre-merge coverage. And Doc 15 §7 runs every founder demo 'on the live preview' — the S3 week-8 obligations-dashboard moment depends on the cadence tick actually ticking in a preview branch.
findings.refs: Doc 13 §1, §4, §5 · Doc 12 §2, §4 · Doc 06 §5 · Doc 07 §8 (cron.schedule 'careos_cadence_tick', pgmq.send 'q_evv_isas'), Doc 07 media/buckets · Doc 15 §7
findings.recommendation: Add an S0 story (extend ST-002): (1) a branch-bootstrap script that provisions per-branch Edge Function secrets, Vault rows, and Storage buckets config-as-code on branch creation; (2) an authenticated on-demand tick/drain endpoint ('run cadence tick now', 'drain queue N now') so E2E and demos drive the async backbone deterministically instead of waiting for schedules — this is also what makes the week-8 demo safe; (3) make staging a separate Vercel project with its own production deployment so Vercel Cron actually runs there; (4) explicitly scope the per-PR E2E suite to sync + on-demand-async journeys and pin the schedule-driven and PowerSync-dependent journeys to nightly staging, in Doc 12 §4, so the coverage split is declared rather than accidental. Verify all four platform behaviors in an S0 spike and record the result in the decision log.

findings.title: 'Rollback' is undefined for append-only data: PITR destroys acknowledged writes and forks the audit chain from its WORM anchors, with no reconciliation runbook
findings.detail: Doc 13 §2 says 'rollback is one click' and Doc 13 §3's answer to a bad migration is a 'pre-apply PITR bookmark'. Neither survives contact with the schema's own guarantees. One-click rollback reverts the Vercel build but not the migration (expand-first makes that safe for schema, but not for a migration/backfill that wrote wrong rows). For data damage, the invariants forbid the obvious paths: audit.audit_event and every [AO] table refuse UPDATE/DELETE (app.forbid_mutation, Doc 07 §4; CLAUDE.md invariant 1), so a bad backfill cannot be repaired in place — and PITR to the bookmark discards everything after it, including legitimate writes: acknowledged PowerSync/EVV uploads from caregiver devices (the device's upload queue is already cleared, so the field data is gone permanently — the exact 'lost data' class CareOS exists to eliminate) and audit rows that a daily 02:00 anchor export (Doc 13 §5) may already have committed to WORM storage. Post-restore, audit.audit_anchor rows in WORM reference a last_event_id/root_hash that no longer exists; the chain-verify job then fails, which is a paging alert (Doc 13 §7 'audit-chain verify failure'), and Doc 13 §9's runbook list has no PITR/anchor-reconciliation entry. The quarterly restore drill (Doc 13 §8) restores into an isolated project, so it never rehearses this divergence. Doc 14 §5 correctly calls post-M3 rollback 'a DR event' but doesn't define what the DR event does to the anchors either.
findings.refs: Doc 13 §2, §3, §5, §7, §8, §9 · Doc 07 §4 (audit.audit_anchor, app.forbid_mutation, trg_audit_chain) · Doc 14 §5 · CLAUDE.md invariants 1, 12
findings.recommendation: Add a 'rollback semantics' subsection to Doc 13 §3 with an explicit preference order: (1) forward-fix (corrections/new versions/compensating rows) is the only rollback compatible with [AO]+anchors once PHI exists — bad-migration recovery is a forward-fix by default; (2) PITR is reserved for corruption-class events, and its runbook (add to Doc 13 §9) must cover: quiesce writes, snapshot-diff the discard window (what acked mobile uploads are being destroyed — export them first), record an attested restore/fork event in the decision log, and define the anchor-verification procedure to accept a documented discontinuity marker (WORM anchors can't be deleted, so verification must be fork-aware by design — add a 'restore_event' anchor row type to Doc 07 §4); (3) make one quarterly drill per year rehearse the in-place-restore/anchor-divergence scenario, not only the isolated-project restore. This is also §164.308 contingency evidence, so it belongs in the drill artifact set.

findings.title: OQ4's 'no prod promotions until decided' interim rule collides with ST-004's S0 prod-hardening ACs, and defers the first-ever prod promotion to the highest-stakes moment
findings.detail: The design doc's OQ4 interim rule forbids production promotions until the second-human question is decided (deadline: end of S0). But S0's ST-004 requires prod-project work in the same sprint: 'High-Compliance config on prod project, network restrictions, log drains… AC: config manifest matches live; Security Advisor zero findings.' The plan never defines what a 'promotion' is, so it's ambiguous whether prod platform configuration is allowed under the interim rule — and since Doc 13 §3 applies prod migrations only 'in the promote step', an un-promoted prod project has an empty schema, making 'Security Advisor zero findings' and the config-parity diff of RLS-force settings vacuous rather than verified. Worse, under the resequence + PHI embargo nothing forces a prod promotion until M0 (S7), so following the letter of the plan, the first-ever exercise of 'promotion is one click, rollback is one click', the first prod migration apply (six sprints of accumulated migrations at once), and the first live test of prod log drains all coincide with pilot PHI cutover.
findings.refs: Design doc OQ4 + CEO plan open questions · Doc 15 §4 ST-003/ST-004 · Doc 13 §2, §3 · Doc 00 §4 V1
findings.recommendation: Two plan edits: (1) define 'promotion' in Doc 13 §2 as app-deploy + prod migration apply, and explicitly exempt config-plane hardening — then split ST-004's AC into an S0 part (config manifest applied; drains/Sentry wired for staging; canary harness running vs staging) and a first-promote part (Advisor zero findings on the real schema; prod drains verified). (2) Schedule a named 'prod shakedown promote' story at S1, immediately after OQ4 is decided: promote the real app + migrations to prod with zero users and zero PHI, verify Advisor/drains/parity against a real schema, and thereafter promote routinely every sprint so the one-click promote/rollback muscle is boring long before S7's pilot data arrives.

findings.title: DB-backed feature flags have a bootstrap problem and no fail-safe contract — and no feature_flag table exists in the binding schema
findings.detail: Doc 13 §2 relies on 'feature flags (DB-backed, per-tenant)' to decouple deploy from release, and Doc 12 §9 gates every release on 'feature flags default-safe' — but Doc 07's table inventory has no general feature_flag table (only ai_capability_flag for AI capabilities, Doc 07 §10), so the mechanism the release gate audits is unspecced. The bootstrap race is real: the migration creating a feature's flag row ships in the same promote as the code that reads it; during the Doc 13 §3 promote window, new code can run before its flag row exists (or old code after it does), and nothing defines behavior when the flag lookup fails or the row is absent. A gated risky feature that defaults open on a missing row is exactly the deploy-time incident class flags exist to prevent.
findings.refs: Doc 13 §2, §3 · Doc 12 §9 · Doc 07 §10 (ai_capability_flag exists; no feature_flag) · CLAUDE.md 'feature-flagged if risk > low' (Doc 15 §5 DoD)
findings.recommendation: Add feature_flag DDL to Doc 07 (tenant-scoped, RLS-forced, audited changes like the Doc 09 §2 role-change convention) and write the flag contract into Doc 08 conventions: code-side default is OFF when the row is absent or the lookup errors (fail-closed); the flag row is seeded default-off in the same migration as the feature's schema (removing the ordering race); reads are server-side and cached per-request (no client-visible flag enumeration). Make Doc 12 §9's 'default-safe' gate check that contract mechanically: a CI assertion that every flag referenced in code has a seeding migration and no default-on seed without a decision-log reference.

findings.title: No mobile compatibility-window policy: EAS release train vs server schema evolution is unbounded, and contraction has no measurable precondition
findings.detail: Doc 13 §3's whole policy is one clause: 'additive sync-rule evolution; client migration handlers shipped ahead of contraction'. It never says how many app versions (or days) back the server must keep supporting, there is no forced-upgrade/min-version mechanism anywhere in Doc 10 or Doc 13, and 'ahead of contraction' has no measurable exit condition — with no forced update, the wait for old clients is unbounded, so contractions either never happen or happen while stale clients are live. The dangerous case is specific to this product: a caregiver device offline for days holds queued EVV writes (visit_event.offline_captured, Doc 07 §7; PowerSync upload queue, Doc 08 §6.8); if a contraction lands before that device reconnects, its queued uploads target dropped/renamed columns and the visit data wedges in the upload queue — field data loss risk plus the Doc 13 §7 EVV freshness SLO breach.
findings.refs: Doc 13 §3 · Doc 08 §6.8 · Doc 07 §7 (visit_event.offline_captured) · Doc 10 §6 (offline-first doctrine) · Doc 13 §7 (EVV freshness SLO)
findings.recommendation: Write the policy into Doc 13 §3 and give Doc 10 the UX story: (1) compatibility window = server supports app versions ≤ N-2 EAS releases or 60 days, whichever is longer; (2) enforce at the edge — sync-token/session issuance carries the app-version claim and refuses below-minimum versions with a forced-upgrade screen (new Doc 10 §6 state, needed by S5); (3) contraction precondition becomes measurable: telemetry shows zero active sessions below min-version AND zero pending upload-queue items from below-min clients (PowerSync client parameters make this observable) — add it to the Doc 12 §9 release-gate list for any contraction migration; (4) the S5 PowerSync story (ST-033) should land the version-claim plumbing so the policy is enforceable from the first mobile release, not retrofitted.

findings.title: ST-004's 'log drains live' AC can deadlock with V7's in-flight BAAs; no named fallback for Sentry
findings.detail: V7 (Sentry BAA, log-store BAA) has verify-by 'S0 start', but ST-001's AC accepts 'signed or dated-in-flight'. ST-004 (same sprint) requires drains + Sentry wired with 'config manifest matches live'. If either BAA is still in-flight at S0 close, you either wire prod telemetry to an un-BAA'd vendor (bad posture, though harmless pre-PHI since D-006 keeps PHI out of prod until S7) or fail ST-004's AC as written. The PHI embargo (Doc 00 §4 global rule) does formally protect the compliance outcome, but the plan's own fallback table (Doc 15 §8) pre-prices an 'alternate log store' and never names a Sentry alternative, so a Sentry-BAA failure at S0 means rebuilding the error-tracking half of the observability stack unplanned.
findings.refs: Doc 00 §4 V7 · Doc 15 §4 ST-001/ST-004, §8 · Doc 13 §1 (config manifest), §6 · D-006
findings.recommendation: Split ST-004's AC: S0 = staging/preview telemetry live + prod drain config staged-but-disabled; a 'prod telemetry live' checklist item moves to the first-promote gate (see S9-3) and is conditional on the executed BAA per the vendor register. Add a named Sentry fallback (e.g., self-hosted GlitchTip in-boundary) to Doc 15 §8's pre-priced list.

findings.title: Deploy-time skew window for Server Actions is unhandled: open tabs break at every promote (and every one-click rollback)
findings.detail: Lane C explicitly includes Next.js Server Actions (Doc 08 §1, Doc 06 §4), and Doc 13 §2 promotes atomically with one-click rollback. Server Action endpoints are identified by build-specific IDs: after a promote, any open tab from the previous build that POSTs a Server Action gets a failed-to-find-action error; a one-click rollback re-creates the same skew in reverse for tabs opened since. No doc mentions Vercel Skew Protection, a client version beacon, or a reload strategy (grep: zero hits for 'skew' across the corpus). The affected users are exactly the all-day-tab population — coordinators in the scheduler grid and RNs mid-form — and the failure surfaces as an opaque error on consequential actions (file intake, exports, finalize orchestration), violating the Doc 10 plain-language error doctrine. The design doc promotes freely during business-hours sprints, so this window recurs weekly.
findings.refs: Doc 08 §1 Lane C · Doc 06 §4 · Doc 13 §2 · Doc 10 §4/§7 (error-state doctrine) · absence: no 'skew' handling anywhere in docs 06/08/10/13
findings.recommendation: Three-line plan change in Doc 13 §2 + Doc 10: (1) enable Vercel Skew Protection and verify its availability/behavior on the exact BAA'd plan tier (V2 decides Pro-HIPAA vs Enterprise — record the answer in the vendor register); (2) add a deploy-version beacon to the app shell with a non-blocking 'CareOS was updated — refresh to continue' prompt (Doc 10 shell state); (3) define a typed CAREOS_DEPLOY_SKEW rescue: Server-Action failures of this class render the refresh prompt, never a generic error — and add a Playwright E2E that performs a promote-during-session to Doc 12 §4. Prefer path-versioned Route Handlers (/api/v1, already the Doc 08 §2 convention) over Server Actions for the longest-lived screens.

sections.summary: The plan's long-term posture is unusually self-aware: most accepted debt is written down near a decision, reversibility is healthy (only the already-ratified Supabase coupling sits below 4/5, and every accepted expansion is a 5), and the exit doctrine is real machinery rather than ceremony. The four warnings share one root cause: the binding surface of this project is the repo, but its newest truths live outside it — the ratified sprint order sits in ~/.gstack while docs/15 still states the old order, the builder-continuity story exists nowhere, the exit gap list is unversioned prose, and the Bedrock fallback has never been exercised. All four are cheap to fix at plan stage and expensive to fix in 12 months, which is exactly when a second engineer or a vendor failure would surface them.

findings.title: The plan of record lives outside the governed repo; until D-009 lands, docs/15 states a sprint order the ratified plan contradicts — and the workforce is agents that read only the repo
findings.detail: CLAUDE.md declares 'The complete specification lives in docs/00–docs/15' and the session ritual is 'check docs/00 §3 for decisions newer than your context.' But the ratified resequence (Approach A) and the accepted expansions E1/E3–E6 exist only in admin-main-design-20260721-180844.md and ceo-plans/2026-07-21-careos-phase1-resequence.md under ~/.gstack — outside the repo the constitution defines as law. Doc 15 §3 still schedules mobile shell + PowerSync at S3 and credentials at S5. The design doc enumerates the six D-009 doc deltas as 'required' but — unlike every other open question, which carries 'Owner: Salim, Decide by: X' — the delta list has no owner or date. E4 (the accepted spec-drift CI gate) checks story-ID citations, decision-ID existence, and docs-index freshness, but it can only see in-repo files, so it structurally cannot catch this gap. A coding agent planning S3 today, or a second engineer reading the repo in 12 months, will build the superseded order in good faith.
findings.refs: CLAUDE.md ('spec corpus is law', session ritual) · Doc 15 §3 · design doc 'Document deltas required (D-009)' · CEO plan E4 · Doc 00 §3/§6
findings.recommendation: Make landing D-009 + the six enumerated deltas the first commit of S0 (before any story work), with an owner/date line added to the design doc's delta list now. Commit the design doc and CEO plan into the repo (e.g. docs/plans/) and reference them from Doc 00 §1. Extend E4 with one assertion: every ACTIVE plan file referenced from Doc 00 exists in-repo.

findings.title: The plan un-clones the founder and installs Salim as the new unmitigated bus factor: no builder-side continuity artifact, account escrow, or handover doc exists or is planned
findings.detail: Doc 00 §5's commercial thesis is 'making her removable from the critical path on purpose' — but the same discipline is never applied to the builder. Under confirmed premise P5, one human holds architecture, all ratified decisions, ops, every vendor relationship (BAAs, ISAS contact, 10DLC, Checkr), and the agent harness. Doc 09 §5's custody matrix says where each secret lives and its rotation cadence, but has no 'who else can reach it' column; Doc 09 §3's dual-control break-glass covers the app's owner role, not the OCTSERVICES-side platform accounts (Supabase org, Vercel team, GitHub, vendor dashboards, BAA files). Design-doc Open Q4 names a second human for prod promotion and CODEOWNERS only — not account recovery or engagement continuity. If Salim is unavailable mid-S4, the client cannot even log into Vercel, and the drills whose evidence auditors need (Doc 13 §8) stop. The onboarding reading path for 'an engineer joining the build' (Doc 00 §2) covers the spec well; nothing covers the operational half: live account inventory, in-flight BAA state, state contacts, harness bootstrap.
findings.refs: Doc 00 §2/§5 · Doc 15 §1 vs design premise P5 · design doc Open Q4 · Doc 09 §3, §5 · Doc 13 §8
findings.recommendation: Add an S0 continuity-kit story: (1) dual-control escrow of platform-account recovery credentials mirroring the Doc 09 §3 break-glass pattern, with the client's counsel or the fractional compliance advisor as second keyholder; (2) a HANDOVER.md in-repo (account inventory, BAA/document locations, vendor + state contacts, harness bootstrap steps, current-sprint state pointer); (3) fold account recovery into the Open Q4 decision due end of S0. The weekly one-page status (Doc 15 §7) doubles as the continuity journal if committed to the repo.

findings.title: Exit-runbook honesty rates 3/5: it names Auth as the largest gap truthfully, but the DDL undermines its own exit seam, the gap list is unversioned prose, and the rehearsal validates data egress rather than service continuity
findings.detail: Doc 13 §10's quarterly pg_dump + storage sync + restore-onto-vanilla-PG rehearsal is genuinely good. Three honesty gaps: (1) Doc 07 builds the right seam — app.current_user_id() and app.is_aal2() exist precisely so Supabase-auth plumbing has 2 shim points — then never uses it consistently: form_version_select uses 'fi.created_by = auth.uid()' directly, form_version_insert checks 'author_id = auth.uid()', and app.emit_audit, app.finalize_form, and app.clock_in all call auth.uid() inline. Repeated across 63 policies and ~20 RPCs, the 'Auth swap' grows from a 2-function shim into a full policy-catalog rewrite. (2) app_user.id is a hard FK into Supabase-managed auth.users (Doc 07 §3), and PowerSync verifies tokens via Supabase Auth's JWKS (Doc 08 §6.8) — an auth swap breaks mobile sync too; the runbook's gap list is 'maintained honestly' prose with no named artifact, owner, or drill evidence location (every other drill in Doc 13 §8 stores artifacts for auditors). (3) A restored vanilla-PG copy has nothing setting the JWT claims GUCs, no Storage/Realtime/Vault services, and no branching-based preview CI — so the rehearsal proves the data survives, not that the business can run; the runbook doesn't distinguish these.
findings.refs: Doc 13 §10 · D-001 condition ('exit runbook maintained') · Doc 07 §3.1 (helpers), §4 (emit_audit), §5 (form_version policies, finalize_form), §6 (clock_in) · Doc 08 §6.8 · Doc 06 §1 R1
findings.recommendation: Three plan changes: (a) add a binding Doc 07 §1 convention — policies and RPCs never call auth.* directly; only the app.* helpers may — enforced by a lint rule and a pgTAP probe (grep-class check), applied before the S0 schema-core migration ships; (b) make the gap list a versioned repo artifact (ops/exit-gaps.md) updated by each quarterly drill, with drill evidence stored like every other drill's; (c) define the rehearsal's pass criteria to include an auth-shim smoke test (GUC-based request identity standing in for Supabase Auth) so 'restore rehearsal' means the policies actually evaluate.

findings.title: The Bedrock fallback is a paper fallback: never exercised, its scope (operational failover vs strategic exit) is unstated, and the embedding fallback silently implies a full corpus re-embed
findings.detail: D-002/D-008 hold Bedrock in a minimal AWS account 'not part of the launch boundary unless the fallback triggers' — meaning at trigger time, account setup, AWS BAA, Bedrock model-access grants, and eval re-baselining all happen under duress. The fallback is more real than most (Bedrock hosts Claude, so registry-versioned prompts largely port), which makes not exercising it inexcusable-cheap: no drill anywhere runs the Doc 11 §9 eval gates against Bedrock endpoints — Doc 12 §5's chaos drill and the Doc 13 §9 runbook both define 'model-provider down' as degrade-to-manual via capability flags, which is the correct hours-scale answer but is never distinguished from the weeks-scale Bedrock migration, so the docs let a reader believe hot failover exists. Bedrock's Claude versions also lag the direct API (registry model_default pins may not exist there). Worst case is embeddings: if V5 resolves to Anthropic-partner or OpenAI-BAA, the stated fallback is Bedrock Titan — a different vector space, so every knowledge_chunk row (vector(1024) hardcoded, Doc 07 §10) must be re-embedded and Brain groundedness re-baselined; no re-embed procedure or cost estimate exists anywhere.
findings.refs: D-002, D-008 · Doc 11 §1 (routing table), §9, §10 (failure matrix) · Doc 13 §9 ('Model-provider outage: flip capability flags') · Doc 12 §5 · Doc 00 §4 V5 · Doc 07 §10 (knowledge_chunk vector(1024)) · Doc 15 §8
findings.recommendation: (1) State in Doc 11 §10 that provider-down = degradation (hours) and Bedrock = strategic migration (weeks) — two different runbooks. (2) Add a semiannual provider-failover drill starting after S7: flip the registry model pointer to Bedrock-hosted Claude in staging, run the full CI eval gates, record version/feature gaps into the S10-3 exit-gaps artifact. (3) When V5 resolves, write the embedding-swap recipe (re-embed job over q_ai_jobs, corpus-version bump, Brain eval re-baseline) as part of the V5 closure evidence.

findings.title: Accepted debt is mostly written down, but ~7 deferred items live in prose with no owner, revisit trigger, or register — invisible to E4 and to a one-human team's memory
findings.detail: Debt attached to decisions is well-recorded (R1–R5 in Doc 06 §1; D-008; the design doc's Phase-2 valves each require a decision-log note when exercised; Open Q4's interim rule). But a second class floats in prose: Secure Compute 'now-vs-later' (unbound after S0), SIEM-lite 'scale-triggered upgrade' with no metric defining the trigger (Doc 09 §7), read replica 'Phase 2', Terraform 'optional later', SSO/SAML 'available later', cloud TTS 'deferred', M4 historical backfill 'optional'. Doc 00 §3 logs decisions made, not decisions deferred; Doc 15 §8 is a risk register, not a debt ledger. E4 checks that cited IDs exist — it cannot surface an item that has no ID. On a solo-builder team, un-owned deferrals are the debt most likely to resurface as a surprise (full ledger in artifacts).
findings.refs: Doc 06 §1 R1–R5, §3 (IaC, SSO, TTS rows), §9 · Doc 09 §7 · Doc 13 §8 · Doc 14 §5 M4 · Doc 00 §4 V2 · CEO plan E4
findings.recommendation: Add an 'Accepted debt & deferred decisions' table to Doc 00 (columns: item, where written, revisit trigger, owner) seeded from the artifacts ledger below, and include it in E4's docs-index freshness check so a stale register fails CI. Roll the D-009 entry's doc deltas to include it.

findings.title: COMAR coupling is well isolated as rules-data except one leak: compliance_rule cannot express the 45/90/120 supervisory ladder, forcing Maryland law into app.evaluate_compliance() code — decide this the cheap way at S3
findings.detail: The multi-tenant story is mostly honest: compliance_rule and credential_type are per-tenant data with source_ref, evv_submission has a target column, and feature flags are per-tenant. But compliance_rule.interval_days is a single int (Doc 07 §7), so the medication-involvement-keyed 45/90/120-day supervisory cadence cannot be represented as rule rows — and Doc 07 §7 accordingly specs app.evaluate_compliance() to 'derive due dates from … medication-involvement level' in plpgsql, keyed off the Maryland-specific employee.medication_involvement column (Doc 07 §8). That puts one of the four headline cadences in code, which (a) weakens the surveyor-traceability claim that behavior traces to a source_ref-carrying rule row (Doc 06 §10), and (b) means tenant #2 in another state forks the engine, contradicting Doc 06 §6.5's 'SaaS option open at zero marginal cost' — which already oversells: tenant #2 also costs provisioning flow, a per-state rule pack, and an EVV-aggregator adapter (Sandata/HHAeXchange-class, not ISAS).
findings.refs: Doc 07 §7 (compliance_rule.interval_days, evaluate_compliance description), §8 (employee.medication_involvement) · Doc 06 §6.5, §10 · Doc 08 §6.1 · design doc S3
findings.recommendation: When authoring evaluate_compliance at S3 (zero extra cost then, migration cost later): add a params jsonb to compliance_rule so laddered intervals are rule data (e.g. {'by_medication_involvement': {'administers':45,'assists_self_admin':90,'none':120}}), keeping the engine generic and every behavior traceable to a sourced row. Reword Doc 06 §6.5 to 'schema-level readiness' rather than 'zero marginal cost'.

findings.title: One-year question: Doc 03/04's supersession is defined only from outside (Doc 00 footnote + Doc 06 header) — when docs 01–05 land, nothing inside them marks which sections are dead
findings.detail: The precedence rules are genuinely good (Doc 00 §1 rule 1–4; the † footnote spelling out that Doc 03 §1/§5/§6 remain authoritative while its stack sections are superseded; Doc 06's header restating the same split). But the split lives in two external places, and the recovery task for docs 01–05 (design-doc Open Q1) says 'install them' with no requirement to annotate. A reader — or more likely an agent, which loads Doc 03 §5–6 as instructed by Doc 07's header 'Implements: Doc 03 §5–6' — twelve months from now can implement from a superseded Doc 03/04 section that reads as confidently as the live ones. CLAUDE.md's always-loaded precedence pointer mitigates but depends on the model honoring it under long context.
findings.refs: Doc 00 §1 (precedence rule, † footnote) · Doc 06 header ('Supersedes / Carries forward') · Doc 07 header · design doc Open Q1
findings.recommendation: Make the docs-01–05 installation task include per-section supersession banners inside Docs 03/04 ('SUPERSEDED by Doc 06 §N — see Doc 00 precedence') on the dead sections, and add an E4 assertion that any doc listed as partially superseded in Doc 00 contains at least one banner. One-time, ~an hour, closes the classic implemented-from-the-stale-section failure permanently.

findings.title: PowerSync coupling is contained on the write path but the vendor-failure scenario (distinct from BAA-failure) has no plan, and the fallback is self-hosting the same young vendor's product
findings.detail: The design is right: writes go through PostgREST/RPCs under the user's JWT, so RLS stays the single write authority and the write path is fully portable (Doc 08 §6.8). The read path is not: sync rules are PowerSync's DSL, the client schema and offline queue are SDK-managed, and the moat-claim 'true offline-first' (Doc 06 §10) rests on it. Every documented fallback — D-003, Doc 15 §8 — is 'self-host PowerSync', i.e., the same vendor's product, addressing BAA failure but not vendor failure (PowerSync's HIPAA posture dates to Jan 2026; it is a small company). Doc 13 §9 has a replication-slot recovery runbook but no PowerSync-exit line, and Doc 13 §10's gap list names only Auth.
findings.recommendation: Two cheap moves at S5 (when mobile starts): pin and mirror the self-host edition's artifacts in-boundary so the fallback survives the vendor, and add a PowerSync line to the S10-3 exit-gaps artifact (read-path replacement estimate: sync-rules rewrite + client data layer; write path unaffected). No architecture change needed.
